George Sabine  calls it “anything about politics or relevant to politics.” It is neither pure philosophy nor pure science, but a mix of both together with history. It is  history  in so far as it rests on facts,  philosophy  in so far as it judges values, and  science  in so far as it explains — so a theorist is ‘part historian, part philosopher, part scientist’. Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  shows how it blends moral reasoning with rigorous method. Normative/philosophical (Plato, Strauss): asks what OUGHT to be — justice, rights; it clarifies concepts and sets standards of right/wrong. Among the traditional approaches, the normative (philosophical) approach is the most enduring. Normative approach  ( Plato, Leo Strauss ): prescriptive; deals with justice, rights and liberty. It does two things — clarifies political concepts, and sets ‘standards of right and wrong’ to judge institutions and laws. Strauss held that facts and values are both indispensable. Other traditional approaches:  the  historical  ( Sabine, Machiavelli ) studies politics through its past — Laski: “every thinker is the child of his times”; the  empirical  ( Aristotle, Locke ) describes ‘what is’, not ‘what ought to be’; the  legal-institutional  ( Wheare, Dicey ) studies law, the constitution and government machinery. Model Answer Behaviouralism was the attempt to turn politics into a science by studying how people actually behave, using data and remaining value-neutral. It flourished among American scholars after the Second World War, though it began with  Graham Wallas  and  Arthur Bentley  (1908). Its foundations were  David Easton’s   eight tenets  — regularities, systematisation, technique, measurement, verification, integration, value-neutrality and pure science. Pioneers included  Charles Merriam  (the Chicago School) and  G.E.G. Catlin  (a value-free ‘science of power’). Importance:  it arrested the decline of the discipline, pioneered electoral-behaviour studies (aiding party strategy), and made comparative politics a major field by showing that in developing countries ‘text differs from context’. Decline:  traditionalists like  Leo Strauss  attacked value-neutrality — ignoring values, he said, is like “making no difference between pure and dirty water.” By chasing technique it lost relevance;  Easton  himself admitted scholars sat in ‘ivory towers’. The social upheavals of the 1950s-60s exposed this, triggering the post-behavioural revolution of 1969. Conclusion. Q — Comment on the post-behavioural approach. “It is a synthesis of tradition and behaviouralism.” (UPSC 2016) Gist — the spine to recall Post-behaviouralism (Easton, 1969 ‘Credo of Relevance’): technique is fine, but research must be RELEVANT and value-laden. Two watchwords: Action + Relevance; “better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.” It is a synthesis: traditionalism = thesis, behaviouralism = antithesis, post-behaviouralism = synthesis — NOT a rejection of behaviouralism. It restored values without dropping science → led to the resurgence of political theory. Model Answer Post-behaviouralism was launched by  David Easton  in his 1969 presidential address, the  ‘Credo of Relevance’ . It grew out of dissatisfaction with behaviouralism’s neglect of values and social relevance. Its core slogan was “it is better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.” Easton called for a  ‘creative theory’  built on two parameters —  Action  and  Relevance . Its features: it does not reject values but invites them; theory must help solve social crises; political science is an  applied , not a pure, science; and the intellectual’s responsibility is greater than the natural scientist’s. It is best understood as a  synthesis  — traditionalism (thesis) and behaviouralism (antithesis) resolved into post-behaviouralism (synthesis). Crucially, it does NOT reject behaviouralism; it keeps its methods but adds relevance and values. Conclusion.  By restoring the normative dimension without abandoning scientific method, post-behaviouralism reconciled facts and values and paved the way for the resurgence of political theory.  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  reflects this new ‘creative’ spirit. Q — “Political theory is dead.” Critically examine the debate on the decline of political theory. What, according to David Easton, were its causes? (UPSC 2018) Gist — the spine to recall 1950s claim: classical PT is ‘dead’ — too speculative, out of touch (Easton, The Political System, 1953). Easton’s 4 causes: historicism, moral relativism, method-over-purpose, hyper-factualism. Others: Cobban (lost in both capitalism & communism), Lipset (‘good society achieved’), Strauss (positivism ignores values). Conclude: not death but an eclipse of the normative side — soon revived. Model Answer In the 1950s the ‘new science of politics’ declared traditional political theory to be in decline.  David Easton , in  The Political System (1953) , dismissed it as “mere speculation,” out of touch with political reality. Easton gave  four causes  of the decline:  historicism  (obsession with century-old ideas made the discipline ‘parasitic’);  moral relativism  (values excluded to make politics value-neutral);  confusion of science and theory  (method given primacy over purpose); and  hyper-factualism  (an obsession with facts, producing ‘theoretical malnutrition and a surfeit of facts’). Others joined in:  Alfred Cobban  said theory had lost relevance in both capitalist and communist systems;  Seymour Lipset  claimed the search for the ‘good society’ had ended; and  Leo Strauss  argued that positivism ignored normative issues and ‘obliterated the distinction between men and brutes’. Conclusion.  The ‘decline’ was not the death of political theory but a temporary eclipse of its normative-philosophical side by positivism. As even Cobban admitted, ‘all was not yet lost’ — and Easton himself soon launched the post-behavioural revival. Q — Comment on the resurgence of political theory. Account for its revival since the 1970s. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall From the 1970s, PT bounced back — values returned and science & philosophy were reconciled. Trigger: the post-behavioural turn (1969) — applied science + relevance. Revival of philosophy: Germino (Beyond Ideology) — Oakeshott, Arendt, Strauss, Rawls. Convergence: Rawls uses method for justice; science = means, philosophy = ends. Model Answer After being written off in the 1950s, political theory staged a strong resurgence from the 1970s, marked by the return of values and the reconciliation of facts and values. The turning point was  Easton’s  post-behavioural ‘Credo of Relevance’ (1969), which converted political science from a ‘pure’ to an ‘applied’ science concerned with real problems.  Dante Germino , in  Beyond Ideology: The Revival of Political Theory , showed the grand tradition reviving through  Michael Oakeshott, Hannah Arendt, Leo Strauss and John Rawls . Science and philosophy converged:  Karl Popper  drew value conclusions,  John Rawls  used an empirical device (the ‘original position’) for his principles of justice, and  C.B. Macpherson  challenged the empirical theory of democracy. New concerns — feminism, human rights, environmentalism — reopened value-judgment. Conclusion.  It is now accepted that political science gives us the ‘means’ while political philosophy determines our ‘ends’ — the two are complementary.  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  is the finest fruit of this resurgence, confirming that political theory is ‘not dead’. Q — Comment on the systems approach to the study of politics, and situate it among the other modern and contemporary approaches. (UPSC 2022) Gist — the spine to recall Systems approach (Easton): politics = input → conversion → output → feedback; the ‘authoritative allocation of values’. Strength: a holistic, comparative, self-regulating model of politics. Critique: too abstract, status-quoist, Eurocentric, ignores power and the individual. Other approaches: textual vs contextual (Skinner), Derrida’s deconstruction — no single approach suffices. Model Answer The systems approach, pioneered by  David Easton , was the most influential modern attempt to build a general theory of the political process. Easton treats the ‘political system’ as the mechanism for the  ‘authoritative allocation of values’ . Politics works as a cycle:  inputs  (society’s demands and supports) →  conversion  inside the system →  outputs  (decisions and policies) →  feedback , which generates fresh demands and keeps the system in balance. Strength:  a holistic, comparative and self-regulating model.  Weaknesses:  it is too abstract,  status-quoist  (it favours stability over change), Eurocentric, and neglects power and the individual. Other approaches:  the  textual  approach reads classics literally, while the  contextual  approach (the Cambridge School —  Skinner, Pocock ) reads them in their linguistic context.  Jacques Derrida’s   deconstruction  holds that “no meaning is ultimate — every understanding can be a misunderstanding.” Conclusion.  The sheer range of approaches shows that no single one can capture politics fully; as  Theda Skocpol  urged in ‘bringing the state back in’, a combination is needed to keep the discipline relevant. Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of the liberal theory of the state through its negative, positive and neo-liberal phases, and critically examine the neo-liberal conception of the state and its link with globalization. (UPSC 2016/2017/2018) Gist — the spine to recall Liberal state = a neutral, minimal state that protects individual rights and rests on the people’s consent; it is a ‘necessary evil’. It evolved in 3 phases: negative/laissez-faire (Smith, Bentham) → positive/welfare (J.S. Mill, Green) → neo-liberal/night-watchman (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick). Neo-liberalism rolled back the welfare ‘nanny state’, gave priority to economic liberty, and became the ideology of globalization (Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus). Critique: it deepens inequality and faces a legitimacy crisis → revival of welfare (Sen, Stiglitz). Model Answer The liberal theory sees the state as a  neutral, limited instrument  that exists to protect individual rights and freedom, resting on the  consent of the people .  Paine  called it a ‘necessary evil’ — evil because it restricts freedom, necessary because freedom cannot be safeguarded without it. It evolved in three phases. (i) Negative / classical liberalism  ( Adam Smith, Bentham, James Mill, Herbert Spencer ): the rational individual has inalienable rights to life, liberty and property; the state should follow  laissez-faire , limited to law and order and enforcing contracts — ‘negative liberty’ as the absence of interference. (ii) Positive / welfare liberalism  ( J.S. Mill, T.H. Green, Hobhouse ): since laissez-faire ignored equality, the state becomes an  agency of common good  enabling ‘positive liberty’ — the condition for self-development — through welfare and distributive justice. (iii) Neo-liberalism / libertarianism  ( Hayek, Friedman, Nozick ): a reaction to the interventionist ‘nanny state’. It restores the  night-watchman state , prioritises economic liberty (“economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom” — Friedman) and rejects welfare — for  Hayek , “social justice is a mirage”. Neo-liberalism & globalization.  It became the ruling ideology of globalization — adopted under  Thatcher  and  Reagan , exported through ‘shock therapy’, ‘structural adjustment’ and the  Washington Consensus  (‘trade not aid’), with the  WTO  as its high point — hence “the political ideology of globalization is neo-liberalism.” Conclusion.  By overestimating the individual and underestimating the state, liberalism builds a capitalist order that can serve exploitative ends; neo-liberalism’s widening inequality has produced a  legitimacy crisis , prompting  Amartya Sen  and  Stiglitz  to argue for a balanced, welfare-oriented state — for example, the post-2008 revival of state intervention. Q — Examine the Marxist theory of the state — its origin, its instrumentalist and relative-autonomy (structuralist) variants, and its materialist basis. (UPSC 2013/2014) Gist — the spine to recall For Marxists the state is NOT neutral — it is a class instrument protecting the dominant (capitalist) class. Its basis is materialist: the economic ‘base’ (who owns the means of production) determines the political ‘superstructure’, i.e., the state. Instrumentalist view (Marx, Lenin, Miliband): state = ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’. Structuralist view (Poulantzas, Althusser): the state has ‘relative autonomy’ but in a crisis always sides with the rich; it ‘withers away’ in communism. Model Answer Marxism is a critique of the liberal-capitalist state. Against the liberal claim of neutrality, it argues the state is a  class institution  — an instrument of coercion serving the dominant class. Its origin lies not in a contract but in  force  and the split of society into contending classes ( Engels ). Materialist basis.  Marx’s understanding is materialistic because the state belongs to the  superstructure  that is determined by the economic  base  — the mode of production and the class that owns it. Political power is therefore ‘the organised power of one class for oppressing another’; ideas, law and the state reflect the material interests of the ruling class. Instrumentalist variant  ( Marx, Lenin, Ralph Miliband ): the state is “the executive committee of the bourgeoisie” (Marx) and “represents the irreconcilability of class antagonism” (Lenin).  Miliband , in  The State in Capitalist Society , showed that even the welfare state left wealth concentrated and the bureaucracy/judiciary elitist — exploding the myth of a ‘managerial revolution’. Structuralist variant  ( Poulantzas, Althusser ; rooted in Marx’s  The 18th Brumaire ): the state has  relative autonomy  — where no single class dominates it can act as an ‘equilibrium-maker’ (Bonapartism), appearing neutral. But the autonomy is only relative: in a crisis it always intervenes for the rich (e.g. the 2008 bank bailouts amid ‘Occupy Wall Street’). Conclusion.  The state exists only as long as classes exist and will ‘wither away’ in a classless society.  Robert Dahl  criticises it for assuming all conflict is class conflict and ignoring pluralist competition; yet the Marxist theory remains the sharpest exposure of the class bias hidden behind the state’s claim to neutrality. Q — Critically examine the pluralist theory of the state and sovereignty as an attack on the monistic (Austinian) theory. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Monistic theory (Hobbes, Austin): sovereignty is one, absolute, indivisible and located in the state — ‘law is the command of the sovereign’. Pluralists (Laski, MacIver) reject this: power should be shared among many associations; the state is just one association among many. ‘Since society is federal, authority should also be federal’ (Laski). It is more realistic in an age of federalism, the UN and the EU, but is criticised as inconsistent (anti-state yet keeps the state). Model Answer The  monistic / Austinian theory  holds that in every state there is one determinate,  absolute, indivisible and inalienable  sovereign.  Austin : if a determinate human superior, not obeying any other, receives habitual obedience from the bulk of society, that superior is sovereign and ‘law is the command of the sovereign’ — echoed in  Weber’s  ‘monopoly of legitimate force’. The pluralist attack  ( Laski, MacIver ): power should be  distributed  among the many associations through which people pursue their many interests; the state is one association among many and cannot meet all human needs.  Laski : “since society is federal, authority should also be federal”;  Krabbe : “the notion of sovereignty must be expunged from political theory.” Pluralists come in two grades.  Moderate pluralists  ( Laski ) still make the state ‘the keystone of the social architecture’ because it alone resolves conflict.  Extreme pluralists  ( MacIver ) give it no primacy — the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves” and is ‘both the guardian and the child of law’. Critical evaluation.  Pluralism is more realistic in an age of federalism and international organisations (UN, ICJ, EU), exposing monism as a ‘legal fiction’. But it is charged with  inconsistency  — it attacks the state yet, unlike anarchism, retains it, so critics say ‘pluralists want to keep the cake and eat it too’.  Henry Maine  adds that no real state (e.g. Ranjit Singh’s Punjab) ever fitted Austin’s model. Conclusion.  Inconsistency is not irrelevance: by dispersing power and valuing associations and international law, pluralism is both more realistic and more conducive to peace than the war-prone monistic doctrine. Q — Discuss the theories of sovereignty and examine the challenges posed by globalization to the sovereignty of the modern nation-state. (UPSC 2015) Gist — the spine to recall Sovereignty = the supreme, final law-making power; classically absolute, indivisible and inalienable (Hobbes gave its first full theory). Globalization makes the state’s ‘hard shell’ porous — through technology, markets, international law and global civil society (Ohmae’s ‘borderless world’). Three views: globalists (sovereignty diluted), state-centric (state still in control), transformationalist (Held — not zero-sum). Plus internal challenges: sub-nationalism, multi-ethnic break-ups, nuclear insecurity → crisis of the nation-state. Model Answer Sovereignty — the supreme and final power to make and enforce law — is the defining feature of the modern nation-state.  Hobbes  gave its first complete theory; classically it is  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable  (monistic view), later challenged by the  pluralist  theory of Laski and MacIver. Globalization’s challenge.  If the nation-state is a ‘billiard ball with a hard shell’, globalization makes that shell  porous  — through information technology, market integration, international organisations and law, and a global civil society.  Kenichi Ohmae , in  The Borderless World , argues political boundaries are fading as ‘global citizens’ and transnational firms escape state control. Three perspectives  (no consensus):  globalists  ( Ohmae, McLuhan ) — sovereignty is really diluted, internally and externally;  state-centric  ( Gilpin, Kapstein ) — the world stays state-centric and states control globalization; and the  transformationalist  view of  David Held  — it is ‘not a zero-sum game’: sometimes the state wins, sometimes globalization does.  Sorensen  adds that states are affected unequally. Internal challenges.  The nation-state is also strained from within: stateless nations (the  Kurds ), multi-ethnic break-ups (USSR, Yugoslavia), diaspora loyalties, and the fact that nuclear weapons mean no state can guarantee security — producing a ‘global village’ of shared risks. Conclusion.  Sovereignty is not extinguished but  reconfigured : global problems need global effort, so the state must accept adjustments to its authority — as the EU’s pooling of sovereignty illustrates.  Susan Strange  rightly urges studying economics and politics together to grasp this shift. Q — Analyse the post-colonial theory of the state through the modernization and Marxist (dependency/structuralist) perspectives. (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall Post-colonial theory studies the newly independent ‘third world’ states still shaped by their colonial past (neo-colonialism — Nkrumah). Their twin task is nation-building (a shared identity) + state-building (effective authority). Modernization view: Riggs’ ‘prismatic society’ and Myrdal’s ‘soft state’ (India). Marxist view: dependency theory (Frank, Wallerstein — core vs periphery, ‘development of underdevelopment’) and Alavi’s ‘overdeveloped state’. Model Answer Post-colonial theory is not a fresh theory of the state but an attempt to analyse the  newly independent ‘third world’ states  that remain shaped by colonialism — a continuing ‘neo-colonialism’, a term coined by  Kwame Nkrumah . Scholars like  Edward Said  and  Gayatri Spivak  stress the colonial legacy. These states face a  twin task : nation-building (transferring loyalty from tribe/village to a central polity) and state-building (an effective centre of law and order and welfare). Modernization perspective  (Western/World-Bank scholars): these societies prosper only by integrating with the world economy.  F.W. Riggs  describes them as  ‘prismatic societies’  in transition — marked by formalism, poly-communalism, overlapping functions and the ‘bazaar-canteen’ and ‘sala’ models.  Gunnar Myrdal , in  Asian Drama , calls India a  ‘soft state’  — unable to enforce its laws, so even Nehru could not push land reforms. Marxist perspective.  The  dependency / instrumentalist  approach ( A.G. Frank, Samir Amin, Wallerstein ) divides the capitalist ‘world system’ into a rich  core  and a dependent  periphery  locked in unequal exchange — the ‘development of underdevelopment’ — whose escape lies in  de-linking . The  structuralist  approach of  Hamza Alavi  calls the post-colonial state  ‘overdeveloped’ : because the modern state was an  imported institution  grafted onto a traditional base, its bureaucracy and military tower over society — Pakistan as a ‘military-bureaucratic oligarchy’, India as ‘inspector raj’. It is therefore autonomous, not the instrument of any single class. Conclusion.  Read together, the two perspectives show the post-colonial state as caught between an imported modern form and a colonial economic dependence — which is why nation- and state-building remain its central, unfinished projects. Q — Critically examine the feminist critique of the state. (UPSC 2021) Gist — the spine to recall Feminists argue the state is not neutral but patriarchal — ‘when I look at the state, it appears male to me’ (MacKinnon). Guiding idea: ‘the personal is political’ — the public/private divide hides women’s subordination in the family. Liberal feminists want women included in a neutral state; Marxist-feminists distrust the welfare state as reproducing patriarchy. The state’s male character shows in its reliance on military power; remedy = differentiated citizenship (Young), a feminist foreign policy. Model Answer Feminists challenge the liberal claim that the state is a  neutral  arbiter.  Catherine MacKinnon , in  Towards a Feminist Theory of the State , writes: “when I look at the state, it appears male to me.” The critique rests on the slogan  ‘the personal is political’  — the public/private divide that liberalism defends actually conceals women’s subordination within the family. Streams.  Liberal feminists  see the state as a potentially neutral ally from which women were wrongly excluded and into which they should be admitted.  Marxist-feminists  are sceptical: the welfare state’s benign provision is the cheapest way of ‘reproducing labour power’, reinforcing women’s domestic role and dependence on a male breadwinner, and extending surveillance over reproduction and child-rearing. The critique deepens through  Carole Pateman , whose  The Sexual Contract  exposes the  masculinist bias  of social-contract theory, and  Kate Millett’s  idea of  sexual politics .  Susanne Moller Okin  argues that “without destroying the patriarchal family we cannot get the neutral state.” The male state and its remedies.  Because women are excluded, the state builds its strength on  military power , generating inter-state tension rather than cooperation, and neglecting nature.  Iris Marion Young  answers the false neutrality with  differentiated citizenship ; others (e.g.  Hillary Clinton ) argue for a more humane  feminist foreign policy . Conclusion.  The feminist critique is powerful in unmasking the state’s gendered character, though its streams differ on whether to enter, reform or bypass the state. Its lasting insight is that genuine neutrality is impossible while patriarchy structures the family and public life. Q — Compare the conceptions of the state in Fascism and Marxism, and discuss the Gandhian view and the ‘crisis of legitimacy’ in capitalist societies. (UPSC 2014/2015/2018) Gist — the spine to recall Fascism glorifies the state as an absolute end — ‘nothing against, over or beyond the State’ (Mussolini); Marxism sees it as a temporary class tool that will wither away. So they are opposites: Fascism = state worship; Marxism = eventual statelessness. Gandhi distrusts the state as ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion; his ideal is ‘enlightened anarchy’/Ramrajya. Capitalist states face a ‘legitimacy crisis’ (Habermas): welfare demands outrun what capitalism can fund. Model Answer Fascism  glorifies the state as an  absolute, totalitarian end  in itself.  Mussolini : “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it”; drawing on  Hegel  (‘the State is the march of God on earth’), it builds a corporate, single-party dictatorship with autarky and an expansionist foreign policy.  Laski  dismissed it as an ‘unsystematic doctrine’; Marxists saw it as capitalism defending itself in decay. Marxism , by contrast, sees the state as a  temporary class instrument  — the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’ — that will ‘wither away’ once classes end. Hence the two are  opposites : Fascism ends in state-worship and permanent dictatorship, Marxism in an eventual stateless society; both, however, reject liberal democracy and individual autonomy. Gandhi’s view.  For  Gandhi  the state is  ‘a soulless machine’  resting on coercion (police, courts, prisons) that stunts self-reliance and violates  Ahimsa . Drawing on Thoreau and  Tolstoy , he wants the state dissolved through  Swaraj / self-control  into ‘enlightened anarchy’ and  Ramrajya  built on ‘oceanic circles’ — a view  Ambedkar  rejected, seeing the state as a means of emancipation. Crisis of legitimacy.  Jurgen Habermas , in  Legitimation Crisis , argues capitalist democracies face ‘crisis tendencies’: democratic politics generates demands for welfare and equality that require higher taxation and spending, which constrains capital accumulation — ‘government overload’ ( Anthony King ) and a  ‘crisis of governability’  ( Atul Kohli ). Conclusion.  Across these conceptions the state ranges from a worshipped absolute (Fascism) to a doomed class tool (Marxism) to a coercive machine to be transcended (Gandhi) — while the legitimacy-crisis debate shows even the liberal-capitalist state struggling to reconcile democracy with capitalism. Sen accepts Rawls’ goal but rejects his method: real justice can’t be worked out by abstract people in an imaginary situation.

The shared theme: there is no universal justice — “what is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.” Rawls’ response  ( Political Liberalism ): he accommodates the critique without changing his principles. He  limits their scope to political institutions  — a ‘political, not metaphysical’ conception of justice — and grounds stability in an  overlapping consensus : people holding different comprehensive doctrines (Christianity, Islam, liberalism) can still converge on the same political principles for their own reasons, unlike a mere Hobbesian  modus vivendi . This rests on public reason, reciprocity and toleration (the ‘burdens of judgement’). Conclusion.  The communitarians rightly expose the thinness of the abstract self, but Rawls’ political turn shows his liberalism can coexist with cultural diversity — justice as fairness survives as the shared political framework of a plural society, even if not as a universal metaphysics. Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls. Gist — the spine to recall Nozick says justice is about how you got your holdings, not about a fair ‘pattern’ of distribution. If you acquired, transferred or were compensated fairly, you are entitled to keep everything — taxing it for the poor is ‘forced labour’. So the state must be minimal (a ‘night-watchman’), doing only protection, not redistribution. Critique: it makes the welfare of the poor depend on the goodwill of the rich; it is a critique of Rawls, not a fuller theory. Model Answer Nozick, in  Anarchy, State and Utopia , offers the  entitlement theory  as a libertarian answer to Rawls. Justice is  historical, not patterned : a distribution is just if it arose through just steps, regardless of the resulting shape. He charges that Rawls “compromises liberty for the sake of equality” and violates human dignity. Three principles of entitlement : (1)  just acquisition  — first appropriation so long as no one is made worse off; (2)  just transfer  — voluntary exchange, treating the person as an end (a Kantian point); and (3)  rectification  of past injustice. If holdings pass these tests, the owner has an absolute right to them. Hence  redistribution is illegitimate : “progressive taxation is like bonded labour,” and, echoing  Hayek , ‘social justice is a mirage’. The state must be a  minimal / night-watchman state  — protecting persons and property but with ‘no role in distributive justice’. His one exception is the  single-well  case, where a monopoly threatening life justifies intervention. Example:  Sachin Tendulkar  becoming rich because millions freely pay to watch him is perfectly just. Critique.  The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’ and effectively defends existing oppression in the name of justice; it ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but also to chance. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.” Conclusion.  Nozick powerfully defends liberty and property against Rawlsian redistribution, but by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market — which is why his theory is read more as a foil to Rawls than as a self-standing account of justice. Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach. Gist — the spine to recall Sen accepts Rawls’ goal but rejects his method: real justice can’t be worked out by abstract people in an imaginary situation. He prefers ‘social choice’ (real people, real situations) over Rawls’ ‘rational choice’. Niti (perfect just institutions) vs Nyaya (justice as actually realised in people’s lives) — Nyaya matters more. So focus on removing real injustice and building people’s capabilities, not on designing a perfect blueprint. Model Answer Amartya Sen’s quarrel with Rawls is  methodological , not about goals. He rejects Rawls’  rational choice  — ‘abstract individuals negotiating in abstract situations’ — in favour of  social choice : ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’. Niti vs Nyaya.  Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ is  Niti  — procedural, about designing perfectly just institutions. Sen prizes  Nyaya  — a ‘realization-focused’ justice concerned with how life actually turns out. ‘Substance is more important than procedure’, so Sen’s approach is  consequentialist  where Rawls’ is deontological. He illustrates that there is no single formula with the  three children and a flute : Carla (who can play it) voices the utilitarian claim, Bob (who has no other toy) the socialist claim, and Ann (who made it) the libertarian claim — all reasonable, none absolute. In the  Krishna–Arjun  debate, Sen finds Arjun’s consequentialist worry (‘many lives would be lost’) more compelling than Krishna’s deontological ‘do your duty’. The capability approach.  Sen therefore proposes a  realization-focused capability approach : justice means expanding people’s real freedoms — ‘development as freedom’ — and removing manifest injustice, rather than chasing a perfect institutional blueprint. Conclusion.  Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation. His critique makes justice comparative and practical, better suited to a diverse world where perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon. Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018) Gist — the spine to recall Justice comes in several forms depending on what is being shared or corrected. Distributive justice = fair sharing of resources; David Miller gives 3 principles — rights, desert, and need (need is the most appropriate). Procedural justice = follow fair rules (‘procedure established by law’); substantive justice = a fair outcome (‘due process’). Also: retributive (punishment), and social/political/economic/legal justice. Model Answer Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced. Distributive justice  concerns the fair sharing of resources and opportunities.  David Miller  (in  Social Justice ) gives three principles, each fitting a social order: distribution by  rights  (hierarchical order — Hume), by  desert  (competitive market — Spencer), and by  need  (solidarity community — Kropotkin) — the last being ‘the most appropriate’. Schools differ: classical liberals want minimal intervention,  Nozick  almost none,  Rawls  the difference principle, and  Sen  capability-building. Procedural vs substantive justice.  Procedural justice works ‘at the level of application’ — the letter of the law, equality before law, ‘procedure established by law’ — and inspires the minimal state.  Substantive justice  cares about the  outcome  — the spirit of the law, ‘due process’ — and encourages state intervention. In India,  Maneka Gandhi  expanded Article 21 from procedure to due process, i.e. from procedural to substantive justice. Retributive justice  (rooted in Aristotle, Kant and Hegel) fixes punishment for crime; criticised for ignoring the offender, it yields to  restorative/transformative justice . Justice is also classified as  social  (equal access regardless of circumstance),  political  (power-sharing — suffrage, reservation),  economic  (equal opportunity for a dignified life) and  legal  (enforcement of established law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just). Conclusion.  These dimensions are interlocking: legal and political justice supply the framework, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content — and the modern welfare state, guided by Rawls and Sen, tilts the balance from mere procedure toward substantive, need-based justice. Q — “Justice is an architectonic and dynamic idea.” Discuss its importance in political philosophy and how conceptions of justice have evolved. Gist — the spine to recall Justice is the ‘first virtue of social institutions’ (Rawls) — the master value the whole of political philosophy revolves around. ‘Architectonic’ = foundational; people obey institutions only if they find them just. ‘Dynamic’ = our idea of justice keeps changing — slavery, untouchability and women’s subordination were once ‘justified’, now rejected. It evolved from Plato/Aristotle → Hobbes → utilitarians → Marxists → today’s affirmative-action redistribution. Model Answer Derived from the Latin  jus  (a bond) and  jungere  (to bind), justice ‘binds people into a fair order of relationships by giving each their due’.  Rawls  calls it “the first virtue of social institutions, just as truth is of a system of thought.” Architectonic.  Justice is the  master/foundational value  around which the whole of Western political philosophy revolves —  Plato’s   Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’. Its centrality is practical: people accept and obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underpins political obligation and stability itself. Dynamic.  Though it embodies an ideal ‘akin to absolute truth’, our grasp of justice is ‘a continuous process’ that tracks changing  social consciousness .  D.D. Raphael  calls this ‘modern consciousness’: slavery and serfdom were once ‘justified’ in Europe, untouchability in India, the subordination of women everywhere — all now condemned. A conception of justice must therefore rest on  reason  read in the light of the prevailing social consciousness. Evolution.  Conceptions have shifted from  Plato  (one’s natural station) and  Aristotle  (proportional equality) through  Hobbes  (justice = obeying the sovereign’s order) and the  utilitarians  (the hedonistic calculus) to the  Marxists  (ending class exploitation) and, today, ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’. Conclusion.  As an architectonic idea justice is the foundation of legitimate political order; as a dynamic idea it is a moving frontier of moral progress — which is why every major theory, from Plato to Rawls and Sen, is ultimately a theory of justice. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Rawls : ‘justice is the first virtue of social institutions’; justice = fairness; deontological (Kantian). Original position  +  veil of ignorance  +  maximin  → choose fair principles not knowing your place. Two principles:  (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + difference principle (help the least advantaged) — in lexical order. Primary goods:  liberty, rights, income, wealth, self-respect. Plato : justice = each doing his own duty (station by nature);  Aristotle : treat equals equally, unequals unequally. Nozick ,  Anarchy, State and Utopia : entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); ‘tax = forced labour’; minimal state. ‘Social justice is a mirage’ = Hayek  (not Nozick — source typo). Amartya Sen : social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya (realization-focused); three children & a flute; capability approach. Communitarians  (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre): the ‘situated self’; ‘justice is the art of differentiation, not homogenisation’. Sandel ,  Liberalism and the Limits of Justice ;  Walzer ,  Spheres of Justice  (complex equality). Rawls’ reply ,  Political Liberalism : political (not metaphysical) conception; overlapping consensus (vs modus vivendi). David Miller : 3 principles of distributive justice — rights (Hume), desert (Spencer), need (Kropotkin). Procedural  (procedure established by law) vs  substantive  (due process); Maneka Gandhi expanded Art.21. The Law of Peoples : Rawls does NOT extend the difference principle between societies; ‘decent peoples’. Carole Gilligan ,  In a Different Voice : ‘ethics of care’ — justice is masculinist. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Rawls (M1):  original position + veil of ignorance + maximin → 2 principles (equal liberty; fair opportunity + difference principle) in lexical order; contractual + distributive; democratic equality. Greek vs Rawls (M2):  Plato (station by nature) & Aristotle (proportional) justify hierarchy; Rawls builds egalitarian, individual-rights justice. Communitarian critique (M3):  Sandel/Walzer/Taylor/MacIntyre — situated self, complex equality; Rawls’ reply = political conception + overlapping consensus. Nozick (M4):  entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); minimal state; tax = forced labour; welfare of poor left to the rich. Sen (M5):  social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya; capability / ‘development as freedom’; three children & a flute. Dimensions (M6):  distributive (Miller: rights/desert/need), procedural vs substantive (Maneka Gandhi), retributive; social/political/economic/legal. Architectonic & dynamic (M7):  first virtue of institutions; evolves with social consciousness (Raphael); Plato→utilitarians→Marx→affirmative action. Killer quotes:  Rawls — ‘each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice’; Sandel — ‘is anything left of the person?’; Walzer — ‘different goods distributed differently’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’. Q — “Equality of outcome, though the most radical face of egalitarianism, threatens liberty.” Critically examine, distinguishing formal equality, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome.
Equality comes in three rising forms: formal (equal in law), of opportunity (equal starting line), of outcome (equal finish).
Formal equality (‘all men are created equal’) is negative — it ends privilege but ignores real capacity.
Equality of opportunity gives ‘an equal chance to become unequal’; equality of outcome makes everyone finish together.
Outcome equality is the socialist ideal but is attacked (Hayek) as needing coercion, killing incentive and threatening liberty.
Egalitarianism holds that ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’. Equality has assumed three progressively radical forms.

The three forms trade off against liberty differently: formal equality is compatible with liberty but hollow; equality of opportunity is the liberal mean; equality of outcome secures the deepest equality but at the cost of coercion — which is why
difference principle is offered as a balance between the two extremes.
Q — Critically examine the schools of thought on equality — liberal (welfare, resources, capability), Marxist, communitarian and multiculturalist.
Liberals debate WHAT to equalise: welfare (utilitarians), resources (Dworkin) or capabilities (Sen).
Dworkin: hold people responsible for their choices but compensate for bad luck they didn’t choose (‘just initial distribution’).
Sen: equalise capabilities — ‘the ability to do what one wants’; ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is deprivation’.
Marxists want to abolish classes; communitarians (Walzer) want ‘complex equality’ across spheres; multiculturalists (Kymlicka) want group rights.
Liberals agree on equality but differ on its ‘currency’.

The schools move outward from the individual to the group: liberals refine what each person should have (welfare→resources→capability), Marxists locate equality in class abolition, and communitarians and multiculturalists relocate it in spheres and cultures — together showing that genuine equality is plural, not simple.
Q — Discuss the dimensions of equality — legal, political, economic and social — and how they combine into formal and substantive equality.
Equality has four practical dimensions: legal, political, economic and social.
Legal + political equality together make ‘formal’ equality (equal rules and votes).
Economic + social equality together make ‘substantive’ equality (real, not just paper, equality).
Formal equality is a fair rule for all; substantive equality relaxes the rule to help the needy.

Formal equality supplies equal rules and votes; substantive equality supplies real, need-sensitive equality of condition — and the modern welfare state’s task is to convert the former into the latter.
Q — “Affirmative action is indispensable to substantive equality yet deeply contested.” Examine the arguments for and against it, with the Indian reservation debate.
Affirmative action = the state actively favouring historically disadvantaged groups (Dalits in India, Blacks in USA).
It is group-based, not individual: a poor Brahmin doesn’t qualify because his community wasn’t historically deprived.
For: it corrects unjust historical inequality and enables the deprived to escape unfair competition (Articles 15, 16).
Against: it compromises merit, is reverse discrimination and hurts self-respect — the courts call it an ‘enabling’, temporary measure, ‘medicine, not daily bread’.

Q — Is liberty a precondition for equality? Examine the relationship between liberty, equality and justice, and evaluate Berlin’s value pluralism.
Libertarians say liberty and equality clash — forcing equality destroys freedom (Hayek, Nozick).
Socialists reverse it — without equality, liberty is empty (‘noble sound and squalid results’ — Hobhouse).
Socio-liberals (Rawls, Sen, Dworkin) say the two can be balanced — justice is the right mix.
Berlin’s value pluralism: liberty and equality are both genuine but sometimes incompatible values — there is no single ranking.
Liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’ values, and three schools read their relationship differently.

argues that fundamental values are ‘universal, plural, conflicting and incommensurable’ — ‘there is no objective criterion to determine their ordering’ (illustrated by the incompatible goods in the lives of a nun and a married woman). He rejects both value monism and value relativism: liberty and equality are both real goods that may genuinely clash.

Liberty is a precondition for equality only when equality is understood substantively — as ‘treating people as equals’ with equal concern. Berlin’s pluralism warns that no single formula can always harmonise them, which is precisely why justice, as the balancing value, remains the central task of political theory.
Q — “Aristotle supports proportionate, not absolute, equality.” Discuss his conception of equality and its relevance to modern substantive equality.
Aristotle: justice/equality means treating equals equally AND unequals unequally, in proportion to their differences.
So he rejects mechanical, absolute equality — treating unequals equally is itself unjust.
He accepted natural inequality (citizens vs slaves, men vs women) and saw perceived inequality as the main cause of revolution.
Relevance: his ‘unequals treated unequally’ is the logic behind modern affirmative action and substantive equality.

he defines just equality as “the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” Hence ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’.

At the same time he was acutely alert to inequality’s dangers — ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’.
His principle that ‘unequals be treated unequally’ is precisely the logic of modern

Aristotle’s proportional equality, though embedded in a hierarchical Greek society, supplies the enduring insight behind today’s welfare state — that real equality often requires differential, need-sensitive treatment rather than identical treatment for all.

Laski  defines equality through four elements: (1) the  absence of special privilege  — ‘the will of one is equal to the will of any other’; (2)  adequate opportunity  for all (especially education, ‘for the power that counts is the power to use knowledge’); (3)  access to social benefits  with no bar of birth; and (4) the  absence of economic and social exploitation . On economic equality he adds it is ‘largely a problem of proportion’. Barker  treats equality as a  derivative value  — ‘derivative from the supreme value of the development of personality’: “whatever rights are guaranteed to me shall also, and in the same measure, be guaranteed to others.” Bryan Turner  (in  Equality ) gives the most comprehensive, modern account — four types: (1)  fundamental equality  of persons (equal human dignity/worth); (2)  equality of opportunity  (open access on merit and talent); (3)  equality of condition  (equal starting points); and (4)  equality of outcome/result  (equalising end-states through law). Conclusion.  Read together, the three show equality maturing from a negative demand (Laski’s end of privilege) to a positive, developmental ideal (Barker’s personality) and finally to a graded modern typology (Turner) that sets up the central debate between opportunity and outcome. Q — “Equality of outcome, though the most radical face of egalitarianism, threatens liberty.” Critically examine, distinguishing formal equality, equality of opportunity and equality of outcome. Gist — the spine to recall Equality comes in three rising forms: formal (equal in law), of opportunity (equal starting line), of outcome (equal finish). Formal equality (‘all men are created equal’) is negative — it ends privilege but ignores real capacity. Equality of opportunity gives ‘an equal chance to become unequal’; equality of outcome makes everyone finish together. Outcome equality is the socialist ideal but is attacked (Hayek) as needing coercion, killing incentive and threatening liberty. Model Answer Egalitarianism holds that ‘equality is always just; only inequalities need justification’. Equality has assumed three progressively radical forms. Formal equality / equality before law : all share a common human essence — ‘all men are created equal’ (US Declaration), ‘men are born free and equal in rights’ (French Declaration) — expressed as legal equality, the cornerstone of the rule of law. But it is  essentially negative : it grants an equal right to dine in an expensive restaurant while ignoring whether one has the money, and cannot touch ‘institutionalised’ discrimination. Equality of opportunity  (proportional equality, found in Plato) concerns  starting conditions  — it amounts to ‘an equal opportunity to become unequal’, accepting natural inequality (talent, effort) while removing social inequality (poverty, poor schooling), so that no one ‘starts the race halfway down the track’. It is the tenet of  social liberalism , realised through education, health and housing. Equality of outcome  is ‘the most radical and controversial face of egalitarianism’ — ‘all runners finish in line together’.  Rousseau  feared inequality would enslave the poor and corrupt the rich;  Marx  captured the ideal in ‘from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs’. The threat to liberty.  Hayek  objects that ‘people are very different, so to treat them equally must result in inequality — the only way to make them equal is to treat them differently’; equality of outcome needs coercive ‘social engineering’, kills incentive and ‘remains utopia’.  Aristotle , conversely, warned that ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but when unequals are treated equally’. Conclusion.  The three forms trade off against liberty differently: formal equality is compatible with liberty but hollow; equality of opportunity is the liberal mean; equality of outcome secures the deepest equality but at the cost of coercion — which is why  Rawls’  difference principle is offered as a balance between the two extremes. Q — Critically examine the schools of thought on equality — liberal (welfare, resources, capability), Marxist, communitarian and multiculturalist. Gist — the spine to recall Liberals debate WHAT to equalise: welfare (utilitarians), resources (Dworkin) or capabilities (Sen). Dworkin: hold people responsible for their choices but compensate for bad luck they didn’t choose (‘just initial distribution’). Sen: equalise capabilities — ‘the ability to do what one wants’; ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is deprivation’. Marxists want to abolish classes; communitarians (Walzer) want ‘complex equality’ across spheres; multiculturalists (Kymlicka) want group rights. Model Answer Liberal school.  Liberals agree on equality but differ on its ‘currency’.  Equality of welfare  (utilitarians) equates welfare with pleasure;  Ronald Dworkin  (in  Sovereign Virtue ) rejects this for  equality of resources , holding that ‘equality is more fundamental than liberty — liberty is hollow without it’. Dworkin  holds people responsible only for choices made in  chosen  circumstances, not  unchosen  ones, and supports a  just initial distribution : his ‘envy test’, ambition- and endowment-sensitive auction, and the distinction between  brute luck  (compensated) and  option luck  (not) aim at an ‘equitable, not merely equal’ distribution. Amartya Sen  (refined by  Martha Nussbaum ) urges  equality of capability  — ‘the ability to do what one wants to do’ — because people differ in converting resources into functionings. It is social-choice based and realization-focused: ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is a deprivation’, and development is ‘freedom’. Marxist school.  Marx  makes the abolition of classes central — ‘we want to abolish classes, and in this sense we are for equality’ — which is impossible without abolishing private ownership of the means of production.  Communitarians  (Walzer) argue for  complex equality : ‘sometimes we equalise people by differentiating’, blocking advantage in one sphere (wealth) from buying advantage in another (health, office).  Multiculturalists  (Kymlicka, Parekh) demand  group rights , Kymlicka’s ‘luck egalitarianism’ treating minority-culture birth as ‘bad brute luck’ deserving special protection. Conclusion.  The schools move outward from the individual to the group: liberals refine what each person should have (welfare→resources→capability), Marxists locate equality in class abolition, and communitarians and multiculturalists relocate it in spheres and cultures — together showing that genuine equality is plural, not simple. Q — Discuss the dimensions of equality — legal, political, economic and social — and how they combine into formal and substantive equality. Gist — the spine to recall Equality has four practical dimensions: legal, political, economic and social. Legal + political equality together make ‘formal’ equality (equal rules and votes). Economic + social equality together make ‘substantive’ equality (real, not just paper, equality). Formal equality is a fair rule for all; substantive equality relaxes the rule to help the needy. Model Answer Equality operates across four dimensions, which combine into the master pair of  formal  and  substantive  equality. Legal equality  grants equal legal status to all — the  rule of law  plus ‘equality before law’ and ‘equal protection of law’.  Rousseau  saw it as the primary mark of an equal society. Its limit: it is ‘meaningless without equal opportunity to get justice — all may possess equal rights but not equal power to vindicate them’. Political equality  means equal political rights on a ‘one person, one vote’ basis, with no bar to office.  Lipson  notes the ‘many have always been governed by the few’; inequality here has rested on knowledge (Plato), birth (aristocracy), money (plutocracy) and race — and real power may still vest in the bureaucracy, police and army. Economic equality  seeks a ‘level playing field’ of access to wealth.  R.H. Tawney : ‘equality of opportunity is not simply legal equality — it depends on the presence of abilities, not merely the absence of disabilities’;  Laski  adds it is ‘a problem of proportion’ met through differential taxation and social expenditure.  Social equality  ends discrimination by caste, creed, religion, sex, etc., and is ‘enhanced by affirmative action’. The combinations.  “Legal and political equality together form  formal equality ; social and economic equality together form  substantive equality .” The queue captures it: ‘first come, first served’ is formal equality, while a separate queue for the elderly or differently-abled marks the shift to substantive equality. Conclusion.  Formal equality supplies equal rules and votes; substantive equality supplies real, need-sensitive equality of condition — and the modern welfare state’s task is to convert the former into the latter. Q — “Affirmative action is indispensable to substantive equality yet deeply contested.” Examine the arguments for and against it, with the Indian reservation debate. Gist — the spine to recall Affirmative action = the state actively favouring historically disadvantaged groups (Dalits in India, Blacks in USA). It is group-based, not individual: a poor Brahmin doesn’t qualify because his community wasn’t historically deprived. For: it corrects unjust historical inequality and enables the deprived to escape unfair competition (Articles 15, 16). Against: it compromises merit, is reverse discrimination and hurts self-respect — the courts call it an ‘enabling’, temporary measure, ‘medicine, not daily bread’. Model Answer Affirmative action is ‘positive intervention by the state — welfare policies in favour of the disadvantaged’. It targets the  historically disadvantaged  (Dalits in India, Blacks in the USA) and is  class/community-based, not individual : a poor Brahmin does not qualify because his community suffered no historical disadvantage (though he may under poverty-alleviation schemes). It must be distinguished from a mere  preferential policy  for dominant groups (e.g. Jats in Haryana, Marathas in Maharashtra). Arguments for.  It is compensatory / positive discrimination on ‘reasonable and relevant grounds’; it corrects  unjust historical inequalities  and lets the deprived ‘escape tough competition’, grounded in  Articles 15 and 16  of the Constitution — the engine of substantive equality. Arguments against.  Neo-conservatives  hold equality means only equality of opportunity, and that quotas ‘erode respect for merit’; it is ‘inimical to  procedural justice ’ (advantaged Blacks and women may edge out poor Whites and men); the present generation is ‘not responsible for past injustice’ (a departure from substantive justice); and it hurts  self-respect , breeding a ‘feeling of inferiority’. The Indian debate.  Ramachandra Guha  says reservation debates ‘generate more heat than light’;  Pratap Bhanu Mehta  that ‘reservation makes us immoral’. The courts frame it as  temporary and enabling : the  Ram Singh (Jat)  case ordered the government to keep identifying genuinely vulnerable classes, and the  Ashok Kumar  case held reservation is ‘the medicine, not the daily bread’. Conclusion.  Affirmative action is indispensable for converting formal into substantive equality, but its legitimacy depends on staying  targeted, time-bound and evidence-based  — correcting historical wrong without hardening into a permanent entitlement. Q — Is liberty a precondition for equality? Examine the relationship between liberty, equality and justice, and evaluate Berlin’s value pluralism. Gist — the spine to recall Libertarians say liberty and equality clash — forcing equality destroys freedom (Hayek, Nozick). Socialists reverse it — without equality, liberty is empty (‘noble sound and squalid results’ — Hobhouse). Socio-liberals (Rawls, Sen, Dworkin) say the two can be balanced — justice is the right mix. Berlin’s value pluralism: liberty and equality are both genuine but sometimes incompatible values — there is no single ranking. Model Answer Liberty, equality and justice are interdependent yet ‘essentially contested’ values, and three schools read their relationship differently. Libertarians / classical liberals  ( Locke, Smith, Bentham, Nozick, Hayek ) hold liberty and equality to be  contradictory , giving liberty priority and confining equality to legal equality and equality of opportunity.  Hayek : ‘people are very different, so treating them equally must produce inequality; equality before law leads to material inequality’. Socialists / Marxists  reverse the order — equality trumps a ‘bourgeois’ liberty; without material equality, freedom is a privilege of the propertied.  Hobhouse  captures the point: ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. Socio-liberals / egalitarians  ( Rawls, Sen, Dworkin ) deny any necessary conflict.  Rawls  reconciles them in  lexical order ;  Dworkin  through endowment- and ambition-sensitive distribution;  Sen  through ‘development as freedom’. So liberty is not the enemy of equality but, properly understood, a precondition of a meaningful, equal life. Berlin’s value pluralism.  Isaiah Berlin  argues that fundamental values are ‘universal, plural, conflicting and incommensurable’ — ‘there is no objective criterion to determine their ordering’ (illustrated by the incompatible goods in the lives of a nun and a married woman). He rejects both value monism and value relativism: liberty and equality are both real goods that may genuinely clash. Conclusion.  Liberty is a precondition for equality only when equality is understood substantively — as ‘treating people as equals’ with equal concern. Berlin’s pluralism warns that no single formula can always harmonise them, which is precisely why justice, as the balancing value, remains the central task of political theory. Q — “Aristotle supports proportionate, not absolute, equality.” Discuss his conception of equality and its relevance to modern substantive equality. Gist — the spine to recall Aristotle: justice/equality means treating equals equally AND unequals unequally, in proportion to their differences. So he rejects mechanical, absolute equality — treating unequals equally is itself unjust. He accepted natural inequality (citizens vs slaves, men vs women) and saw perceived inequality as the main cause of revolution. Relevance: his ‘unequals treated unequally’ is the logic behind modern affirmative action and substantive equality. Model Answer Aristotle’s conception of equality is  proportional, not arithmetical . In the  Politics  he defines just equality as “the treating of equals equally and of unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities.” Hence ‘injustice arises not only when equals are treated unequally, but also when unequals are treated equally’. This makes equality a matter of  desert and proportion : in distributive justice, honours and wealth should be shared according to relevant merit, not divided identically. He thereby rejects  absolute / mechanical equality  as itself a source of injustice. Aristotle also accepted a good deal of  natural inequality : he distinguished citizens from slaves and men from women in ‘rational and civic capacity’, restricting participation in the Polis to citizens, and even held slavery to be ‘good for both master and slave’. At the same time he was acutely alert to inequality’s dangers — ‘inequality, real or imagined, is the main cause of revolution’. Relevance.  His principle that ‘unequals be treated unequally’ is precisely the logic of modern  substantive equality  and  affirmative action : relaxing a uniform rule to help the disadvantaged (reservations, progressive taxation, special provisions) treats unequals unequally so as to produce genuine, not merely formal, equality. Conclusion.  Aristotle’s proportional equality, though embedded in a hierarchical Greek society, supplies the enduring insight behind today’s welfare state — that real equality often requires differential, need-sensitive treatment rather than identical treatment for all. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Meaning:  negative = end of privileges; positive = opportunity to develop personality; ‘essentially contested’. Laski : equality = no privilege + adequate opportunity + access to social benefits + no exploitation; economic equality = ‘problem of proportion’. Barker : equality is a ‘derivative value’ from the development of personality. Bryan Turner ,  Equality : 4 types — fundamental, opportunity, condition, outcome. Three forms:  formal (‘all men created equal’) → opportunity (‘equal chance to become unequal’) → outcome (all finish together). Marx : ‘from each according to ability, to each according to needs’; ‘abolish classes’. Hayek : treating different people equally must yield inequality; outcome equality needs coercion. Liberal currencies:  welfare (utilitarians) / resources (Dworkin) / capability (Sen). Dworkin ,  Sovereign Virtue : brute vs option luck; envy test; just initial distribution. Sen : capability = ‘ability to do what one wants’; ‘fasting is a choice, hunger is deprivation’; development as freedom. Walzer : complex equality — ‘block the exchanges’ across spheres;  Kymlicka : group rights, ‘luck egalitarianism’. Dimensions:  legal + political = formal equality; social + economic = substantive equality. R.H. Tawney : opportunity depends on ‘presence of abilities, not just absence of disabilities’. Affirmative action:  group-based, historically disadvantaged; Arts.15 & 16; Ashok Kumar — ‘medicine, not daily bread’. Hobhouse : ‘liberty without equality is a name of noble sound and squalid results’. Isaiah Berlin : value pluralism — values are ‘plural, conflicting and incommensurable’; no objective ordering. Aristotle : treat equals equally, unequals unequally; inequality = main cause of revolution. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Meaning & thinkers (MQ1):  negative/positive meaning; Laski (4 elements), Barker (derivative value), Turner (4 types). Three forms (MQ2):  formal (negative, legal) → opportunity (‘equal chance to become unequal’) → outcome (radical, socialist; Hayek’s liberty critique). Schools (MQ3):  liberal currencies welfare/resources(Dworkin)/capability(Sen); Marxist (abolish classes); communitarian (Walzer complex equality); multiculturalist (Kymlicka group rights). Dimensions (MQ4):  legal + political = formal; social + economic = substantive; queue example. Affirmative action (MQ5):  group-based; for = corrects historical wrong (Arts.15/16); against = merit/reverse discrimination/self-respect; enabling & temporary. Liberty-equality-justice (MQ6):  libertarian (clash) vs socialist (equality first) vs socio-liberal (balance: Rawls/Sen/Dworkin); Berlin’s value pluralism. Aristotle (MQ7):  proportional not absolute equality; ‘unequals treated unequally’ → logic of modern affirmative action. Killer quotes:  Hobhouse — ‘noble sound, squalid results’; Hayek — ‘treat them equally → inequality’; Marx — ‘to each according to needs’; Aristotle — ‘unequals treated equally = injustice’. Previous Year Questions — coverage map Equality of outcome as a political idea → MQ2. Affirmative Action / Explain equality → MQ5 (+ MQ4). Aristotle’s conception of Equality → MQ7. Liberty as a precondition for equality; equality–liberty relationship → MQ6. Berlin’s notion of value pluralism → MQ6. (Foundational: meaning & thinkers, schools, dimensions → MQ1/MQ3/MQ4.)

title: 10 - Western Political Thought

content.text: Syllabus — Western Political Thought: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, John S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci, Hannah Arendt. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 10)

the canon of Western political thinkers — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, J.S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci and Hannah Arendt — their central ideas, the comparisons the syllabus draws (Plato vs Aristotle, Hobbes vs Locke, Marx vs Gramsci) and their critiques.

Plato (justice, philosopher-king, Popper critique), Aristotle (constitutions, revolution), Machiavelli (realism, virtu-fortuna), Hobbes (Leviathan, sovereignty), Locke (natural rights, limited state), Mill (liberty, harm principle), Marx (materialism, alienation, surplus value), Gramsci (hegemony), Arendt (vita activa, banality of evil).
Q — Examine Plato’s conception of justice, education, communism and the philosopher-king, and evaluate Popper’s charge that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’. (UPSC 2015)
Plato’s justice = each class doing its own job (rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce) in harmony.
Education creates this ideal state; rulers are wise ‘philosopher-kings’ who alone should rule.
Communism of property and wives (for rulers & guardians only) removes selfish temptations.
Popper attacks all this as totalitarian — an ‘enemy of the open society’ who froze change and freedom.
is ‘each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only’ — a

mirroring the three parts of the soul (reason, spirit, appetite) and the three classes (rulers, guardians, producers) of the ‘myth of the metals’. ‘Justice is the architectonic principle’ and ‘the state is the individual writ large’.
, a lifelong sieve that culminates, at 50, in the rule of the

— ‘until philosophers are rulers or rulers learn philosophy, there is no end to the ills of states’. ‘It is foolish to limit an expert physician with the book of medicine’ — so the philosopher-king rules by wisdom, not law.
To free the guardians from private temptation, Plato prescribes
— but only for the two ruling classes — an ‘economic solution to a political ailment’ (unlike Marx’s economy-wide, economically-motivated communism).
The Open Society and Its Enemies
) charges that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’ — his rigid class order, censorship and rule by an unaccountable elite amount to
, freezing change (‘arrest all political change; change is evil, rest divine’). Bertrand Russell too ‘dubbed Plato a totalitarian’.

Popper’s charge is powerful but arguably anachronistic — defenders like Levinson hold that ‘fascism and Platonism are incomparable’. Whatever the verdict, as Whitehead said, all Western philosophy is ‘footnotes to Plato’ — his linkage of knowledge, virtue and rule remains the founding statement of political philosophy.
Q — Analyse Aristotle’s critique of Plato’s idealism, and contrast their theories of justice and the state. (UPSC 2019)
Aristotle, Plato’s student, replaced his teacher’s idealism with realism — ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’.
He rejected Plato’s ‘one man, one job’ justice and his communism as impractical and against human nature.
Plato’s justice is inner/moral (duties); Aristotle’s is external/legal (proportionate, rights-based).
Both see the state as key to the good life, but Plato idealises it while Aristotle studies it empirically.
Aristotle, Plato’s pupil for twenty years, ‘rectified the limitations of Plato’s ideas’ by replacing idealism with
— ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’ (Will Durant: ‘as Brutus loved Rome more, so for Aristotle dear is Plato, but dearer is truth’).
(a separate ‘world of ideas’) as unreal; his
of ‘one man, one job’ makes life ‘monotonous’, is too subjective/moral rather than legal, and stresses duties over rights. He attacked Plato’s
: ‘what is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — ‘everyone’s property is no one’s responsibility’ — and defended the family as a ‘time-tested institution’ of emotional stability.
(harmony of the soul, duties); for Aristotle it is
— ‘proportionate equality’: ‘it is unjust to treat equals unequally and unequals equally’, divided into distributive and corrective justice.

Both hold the state essential to the good life (Plato: ‘the greatest happiness of the whole’; Aristotle: ‘man is by nature a political animal’, the state exists ‘for the sake of the good life’). But Plato is the
designing an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings, whereas Aristotle is the
who studied 158 constitutions and preferred the rule of law and a middle-class ‘polity’.

Aristotle’s realism corrects Plato’s idealism — from an ideal to be constructed to institutions to be studied and improved — which is why he, not Plato, is called the ‘father of political science’, even as both remain rooted in the shared Socratic conviction that the state exists for human excellence.
Q — Explain Aristotle’s classification of constitutions, his theory of proportionate equality and revolution, and assess his contribution to modern constitutional democracy. (UPSC 2021/2017)
Aristotle classified governments by how many rule and whether they rule for the common good.
Six types: correct (kingship, aristocracy, polity) and their perverted forms (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).
‘Polity’ (rule of the many via the middle class) is the golden mean and the most stable.
Revolution springs from a sense of inequality ‘real or imagined’; his ideas feed modern rule of law and constitutionalism.
Aristotle, the ‘father of comparative politics’ who studied 158 constitutions, classified governments on two axes — the
and whether they rule for the
— is the most stable and practicable, since the middle class moderates the conflict of rich and poor.
Justice requires ‘treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’ —

‘The feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’, and ‘poverty is the parent of revolution and crime’. Aristotle catalogued the general and regime-specific causes and cures of revolution, counselling moderation and the strengthening of the middle class — a conservative concern for
over the rule of persons (‘law is reason without passion’), the
, and constitutional stability directly anticipate modern constitutional democracy — though his exclusion of women, workers and slaves from citizenship is ‘unacceptable in modern times’.

Aristotle’s empirical, moderate and law-centred vision — government for the common good, balanced by the middle class and bound by law — is the classical seed of modern constitutional democracy, even as its citizenship must be democratised to meet modern standards of equality.
Q — Critically examine Machiavelli’s separation of politics from ethics and religion, and his place in the evolution of political science. (UPSC 2018/2014)
Machiavelli separated politics from morality and religion — the first to justify ‘dirty hands’ for the state’s sake.
He judged rulers by success, not virtue: a prince must ‘know how to be bad’ and combine the lion and the fox.
Religion is useful as a tool of discipline — ‘use religion, don’t get used by it’.
By studying politics as it IS (empirically), he became the ‘father of political realism/modern political science’.
by divorcing politics from ethics and religion and judging action by its
, not its morality — the first to justify ‘dirty hands’ in statecraft.

Given a selfish human nature (‘men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’), the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad rather than good’ and must combine ‘the courage of the
’, changing colours ‘like a chameleon’. On the safer bet: ‘it is better for a prince to be
— as a disciplinary, unifying force: the ruler should ‘use religion rather than get used by it’. This makes him, for the text, the ‘father of European secularism’.
to human affairs — studying states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’ — Machiavelli marks a decisive break from medieval theology.
called him ‘the Galileo of politics’, and ‘if Machiavelli was Copernicus, Hobbes was the Galileo of political theory’.
He is condemned as ‘the most universally reprobated figure’ (Maxey), an amoral cynic;
finds him ‘narrowly dated and narrowly located’ in Renaissance Italy, and
saw the separation of ethics from politics as a ‘death trap’.

Whatever the moral verdict, Machiavelli’s realism and empiricism made politics an autonomous, observable domain — which is why, despite universal condemnation, ‘everyone practises Machiavellism without confessing it’ (Dunning), and he stands at the threshold of modern political science.
Q — Discuss Hobbes’ derivation of the state from human nature and the state of nature, his theory of absolute sovereignty and political obligation, and compare him with Machiavelli. (UPSC 2017)
Hobbes starts from a selfish, fearful human nature with an ‘endless desire for power’.
Without a state, life is a ‘war of all against all’ — ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’.
So people make ONE contract surrendering all rights to an absolute sovereign (the Leviathan) — obligation is total and irrevocable.
Like Machiavelli he is a realist, but Hobbes builds a systematic theory of sovereignty, not just advice to a prince.
Hobbes, using the ‘resolutive-compositive’ method, derives the state logically from
: man has an ‘endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’ — he is selfish, materialistic and driven by
Absent a common power, this produces a
‘war of every man against every man’
, where life is ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’, driven by competition, diffidence and glory.
To escape it, men make a
their natural rights to a ‘common power’ — creating society and state at once. The resulting
is ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable and perpetual’; ‘law is the command of the sovereign’ (anticipating Austin), and ‘covenants without the sword are but words’.
Because the covenant is made among the subjects (not with the sovereign), obligation to obey is
— yet it is grounded in consent for
, so the one right that cannot be surrendered is the right to life; if the sovereign cannot protect it, obligation lapses.
who reject classical natural sociability and a moralised politics. But Machiavelli offers
whose goal is glory, while Hobbes builds a
whose goal is escape from the state of nature through absolute sovereignty.
Hobbes converts Machiavellian realism into a rigorous science of the state.

reads him as the ‘scholar of possessive individualism’ whose theory fits a ‘possessive market society’ — yet by grounding the state in consent and self-preservation, Hobbes is also, paradoxically, a father of modern individualism.
Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority.
Locke’s state of nature is peaceful but ‘inconvenient’ (no impartial judge), so people set up government.
They make TWO contracts and transfer only limited powers — creating a limited, ‘trust’ state (unlike Hobbes’ absolute one).
Natural rights to life, liberty and property are inalienable; property comes from mixing one’s labour with nature.
So Hobbes justifies an absolute state, Locke a limited constitutional state with a right to revolt — the birth of liberalism.
Locke, the ‘father of liberalism’, begins from a
— reason guides man ‘not to harm others in their life, liberty and property’. His
is ‘a state of peace and mutual assistance’, pre-political but not pre-social, flawed only by two ‘inconveniences’ (men judge in their own case; may act in passion).
Two contracts and the limited state.
— one forming civil society, another forming a government by
— and transfer only the powers to make, execute and adjudicate law. The state thus holds
, not original power: a ‘night-watchman’ state whose ‘sole purpose is the protection of property’, with separation of powers (legislative supreme, executive, federative) and a
against a government that betrays its trust.
, ‘property is the product of one’s labour’, subject to limits (no spoilage, enough left for others). His
defends freedom of conscience — though, notably, not for atheists.
Both use contract, but from opposite premises:
sovereign, ‘liberty where the law is silent’;
Where Hobbes legitimizes state authority as
(to escape chaos), Locke legitimizes it as
(to secure pre-existing rights) — which is why Locke, the ‘individualist out and out’, founds the liberal-constitutional tradition that runs through to Rawls.

Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021)
Mill revised utilitarianism by adding quality — ‘better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’.
His ‘harm principle’: the state may restrict a person only to prevent harm to others.
He fiercely defended free speech — ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’.
A ‘reluctant democrat’, he feared the ‘tyranny of the majority’; and (with Harriet Taylor) he championed women’s equality.
dimension — ‘it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’ — rescuing it from Bentham’s ‘pig’s philosophy’.
Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. His
holds that ‘the sole end for which mankind is warranted in interfering with the liberty of a person is to prevent harm to others’ — distinguishing self-regarding from other-regarding action.

‘All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’ — even one dissentient must be heard, for the silenced opinion may be true, or contain part of the truth; hence his defence of the ‘crank’ whose rare genius benefits mankind.
calls Mill a ‘reluctant democrat’: fearing the
