Syllabus — Western Political Thought: Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, John S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci, Hannah Arendt. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 10)







Unit Snapshot

What this unit covers: the canon of Western political thinkers — Plato, Aristotle, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, J.S. Mill, Marx, Gramsci and Hannah Arendt — their central ideas, the comparisons the syllabus draws (Plato vs Aristotle, Hobbes vs Locke, Marx vs Gramsci) and their critiques.

Must-know anchors: Plato (justice, philosopher-king, Popper critique), Aristotle (constitutions, revolution), Machiavelli (realism, virtu-fortuna), Hobbes (Leviathan, sovereignty), Locke (natural rights, limited state), Mill (liberty, harm principle), Marx (materialism, alienation, surplus value), Gramsci (hegemony), Arendt (vita activa, banality of evil).

PYQ trend: Plato/Popper (2015), Aristotle (2015/2017/2019/2021), Machiavelli (2014/2018), Hobbes (2017), Mill (2014/2018/2021), Marx (2015/2016/2020), Gramsci (2013/2015/2016/2019), Arendt (2019).

Master Questions







Q — Examine Plato’s conception of justice, education, communism and the philosopher-king, and evaluate Popper’s charge that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’. (UPSC 2015)





Gist — the spine to recall





Plato’s justice = each class doing its own job (rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce) in harmony.



Education creates this ideal state; rulers are wise ‘philosopher-kings’ who alone should rule.



Communism of property and wives (for rulers & guardians only) removes selfish temptations.



Popper attacks all this as totalitarian — an ‘enemy of the open society’ who froze change and freedom.





Model Answer

For Plato (in The Republic) justice is ‘each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only’ — a functional harmony mirroring the three parts of the soul (reason, spirit, appetite) and the three classes (rulers, guardians, producers) of the ‘myth of the metals’. ‘Justice is the architectonic principle’ and ‘the state is the individual writ large’.

Education and the philosopher-king. Justice is realised through state-sponsored education, a lifelong sieve that culminates, at 50, in the rule of the philosopher-king — ‘until philosophers are rulers or rulers learn philosophy, there is no end to the ills of states’. ‘It is foolish to limit an expert physician with the book of medicine’ — so the philosopher-king rules by wisdom, not law.

Communism. To free the guardians from private temptation, Plato prescribes communism of property and wives — but only for the two ruling classes — an ‘economic solution to a political ailment’ (unlike Marx’s economy-wide, economically-motivated communism).

Popper’s critique. Karl Popper (in The Open Society and Its Enemies) charges that ‘Plato was an enemy of the open society’ — his rigid class order, censorship and rule by an unaccountable elite amount to totalitarianism, freezing change (‘arrest all political change; change is evil, rest divine’). Bertrand Russell too ‘dubbed Plato a totalitarian’.

Conclusion. Popper’s charge is powerful but arguably anachronistic — defenders like Levinson hold that ‘fascism and Platonism are incomparable’. Whatever the verdict, as Whitehead said, all Western philosophy is ‘footnotes to Plato’ — his linkage of knowledge, virtue and rule remains the founding statement of political philosophy.







Q — Analyse Aristotle’s critique of Plato’s idealism, and contrast their theories of justice and the state. (UPSC 2019)





Gist — the spine to recall





Aristotle, Plato’s student, replaced his teacher’s idealism with realism — ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’.



He rejected Plato’s ‘one man, one job’ justice and his communism as impractical and against human nature.



Plato’s justice is inner/moral (duties); Aristotle’s is external/legal (proportionate, rights-based).



Both see the state as key to the good life, but Plato idealises it while Aristotle studies it empirically.





Model Answer

Aristotle, Plato’s pupil for twenty years, ‘rectified the limitations of Plato’s ideas’ by replacing idealism with empirical realism — ‘Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend’ (Will Durant: ‘as Brutus loved Rome more, so for Aristotle dear is Plato, but dearer is truth’).

The critique of idealism. Aristotle rejected Plato’s theory of Forms (a separate ‘world of ideas’) as unreal; his justice of ‘one man, one job’ makes life ‘monotonous’, is too subjective/moral rather than legal, and stresses duties over rights. He attacked Plato’s communism of wives and property: ‘what is common to the greatest number gets the least care’ — ‘everyone’s property is no one’s responsibility’ — and defended the family as a ‘time-tested institution’ of emotional stability.

Justice contrasted. For Plato justice is inner, moral and spiritual (harmony of the soul, duties); for Aristotle it is external, legal and practical — ‘proportionate equality’: ‘it is unjust to treat equals unequally and unequals equally’, divided into distributive and corrective justice.

The state contrasted. Both hold the state essential to the good life (Plato: ‘the greatest happiness of the whole’; Aristotle: ‘man is by nature a political animal’, the state exists ‘for the sake of the good life’). But Plato is the idealist/perfectionist designing an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings, whereas Aristotle is the pragmatic realist who studied 158 constitutions and preferred the rule of law and a middle-class ‘polity’.

Conclusion. Aristotle’s realism corrects Plato’s idealism — from an ideal to be constructed to institutions to be studied and improved — which is why he, not Plato, is called the ‘father of political science’, even as both remain rooted in the shared Socratic conviction that the state exists for human excellence.







Q — Explain Aristotle’s classification of constitutions, his theory of proportionate equality and revolution, and assess his contribution to modern constitutional democracy. (UPSC 2021/2017)





Gist — the spine to recall





Aristotle classified governments by how many rule and whether they rule for the common good.



Six types: correct (kingship, aristocracy, polity) and their perverted forms (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).



‘Polity’ (rule of the many via the middle class) is the golden mean and the most stable.



Revolution springs from a sense of inequality ‘real or imagined’; his ideas feed modern rule of law and constitutionalism.





Model Answer

Aristotle, the ‘father of comparative politics’ who studied 158 constitutions, classified governments on two axes — the number of rulers and whether they rule for the common good or self-interest.

Six-fold classification: rule by one — Kingship (correct) vs Tyranny (perverted); by few — Aristocracy vs Oligarchy; by many — Polity vs Democracy. Polity — the ‘golden mean’ identified with the middle class — is the most stable and practicable, since the middle class moderates the conflict of rich and poor.

Proportionate equality. Justice requires ‘treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities’ — proportionate, not absolute, equality, the basis of distributive justice.

Revolution. ‘The feeling of inequality, real or imagined, is the cause of revolution’, and ‘poverty is the parent of revolution and crime’. Aristotle catalogued the general and regime-specific causes and cures of revolution, counselling moderation and the strengthening of the middle class — a conservative concern for stability.

Contribution to modern democracy. His insistence on the rule of law over the rule of persons (‘law is reason without passion’), the mixed/middle-class polity, and constitutional stability directly anticipate modern constitutional democracy — though his exclusion of women, workers and slaves from citizenship is ‘unacceptable in modern times’.

Conclusion. Aristotle’s empirical, moderate and law-centred vision — government for the common good, balanced by the middle class and bound by law — is the classical seed of modern constitutional democracy, even as its citizenship must be democratised to meet modern standards of equality.







Q — Critically examine Machiavelli’s separation of politics from ethics and religion, and his place in the evolution of political science. (UPSC 2018/2014)





Gist — the spine to recall





Machiavelli separated politics from morality and religion — the first to justify ‘dirty hands’ for the state’s sake.



He judged rulers by success, not virtue: a prince must ‘know how to be bad’ and combine the lion and the fox.



Religion is useful as a tool of discipline — ‘use religion, don’t get used by it’.



By studying politics as it IS (empirically), he became the ‘father of political realism/modern political science’.





Model Answer

Machiavelli, writing in The Prince, founded political realism by divorcing politics from ethics and religion and judging action by its results, not its morality — the first to justify ‘dirty hands’ in statecraft.

Politics vs ethics. Given a selfish human nature (‘men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’), the prince ‘needs to know how to be bad rather than good’ and must combine ‘the courage of the lion with the cunning of the fox’, changing colours ‘like a chameleon’. On the safer bet: ‘it is better for a prince to be feared than loved’.

Politics vs religion. Machiavelli treats religion instrumentally — as a disciplinary, unifying force: the ruler should ‘use religion rather than get used by it’. This makes him, for the text, the ‘father of European secularism’.

Place in political science. By applying the empirical method to human affairs — studying states ‘as they are, not as they ought to be’ — Machiavelli marks a decisive break from medieval theology. Ernst Cassirer called him ‘the Galileo of politics’, and ‘if Machiavelli was Copernicus, Hobbes was the Galileo of political theory’.

Critique. He is condemned as ‘the most universally reprobated figure’ (Maxey), an amoral cynic; Sabine finds him ‘narrowly dated and narrowly located’ in Renaissance Italy, and Gandhi saw the separation of ethics from politics as a ‘death trap’.

Conclusion. Whatever the moral verdict, Machiavelli’s realism and empiricism made politics an autonomous, observable domain — which is why, despite universal condemnation, ‘everyone practises Machiavellism without confessing it’ (Dunning), and he stands at the threshold of modern political science.







Q — Discuss Hobbes’ derivation of the state from human nature and the state of nature, his theory of absolute sovereignty and political obligation, and compare him with Machiavelli. (UPSC 2017)





Gist — the spine to recall





Hobbes starts from a selfish, fearful human nature with an ‘endless desire for power’.



Without a state, life is a ‘war of all against all’ — ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’.



So people make ONE contract surrendering all rights to an absolute sovereign (the Leviathan) — obligation is total and irrevocable.



Like Machiavelli he is a realist, but Hobbes builds a systematic theory of sovereignty, not just advice to a prince.





Model Answer

Hobbes, using the ‘resolutive-compositive’ method, derives the state logically from human nature: man has an ‘endless desire for power after power that ceases only in death’ — he is selfish, materialistic and driven by fear (‘fear and I were born twins’).

State of nature. Absent a common power, this produces a ‘war of every man against every man’, where life is ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short’, driven by competition, diffidence and glory.

The contract and sovereignty. To escape it, men make a single contract, each with every other, surrendering all their natural rights to a ‘common power’ — creating society and state at once. The resulting sovereign (Leviathan) is ‘absolute, indivisible, inalienable and perpetual’; ‘law is the command of the sovereign’ (anticipating Austin), and ‘covenants without the sword are but words’.

Political obligation. Because the covenant is made among the subjects (not with the sovereign), obligation to obey is total and irrevocable — yet it is grounded in consent for self-preservation, so the one right that cannot be surrendered is the right to life; if the sovereign cannot protect it, obligation lapses.

Hobbes vs Machiavelli. Both are realists who reject classical natural sociability and a moralised politics. But Machiavelli offers practical advice to a prince whose goal is glory, while Hobbes builds a systematic, deductive theory whose goal is escape from the state of nature through absolute sovereignty.

Conclusion. Hobbes converts Machiavellian realism into a rigorous science of the state. Macpherson reads him as the ‘scholar of possessive individualism’ whose theory fits a ‘possessive market society’ — yet by grounding the state in consent and self-preservation, Hobbes is also, paradoxically, a father of modern individualism.







Q — Evaluate Locke as the father of liberalism through his two contracts, natural rights, labour theory of property and toleration; and contrast with Hobbes on how each legitimizes state authority.





Gist — the spine to recall





Locke’s state of nature is peaceful but ‘inconvenient’ (no impartial judge), so people set up government.



They make TWO contracts and transfer only limited powers — creating a limited, ‘trust’ state (unlike Hobbes’ absolute one).



Natural rights to life, liberty and property are inalienable; property comes from mixing one’s labour with nature.



So Hobbes justifies an absolute state, Locke a limited constitutional state with a right to revolt — the birth of liberalism.





Model Answer

Locke, the ‘father of liberalism’, begins from a balanced human nature — reason guides man ‘not to harm others in their life, liberty and property’. His state of nature is ‘a state of peace and mutual assistance’, pre-political but not pre-social, flawed only by two ‘inconveniences’ (men judge in their own case; may act in passion).

Two contracts and the limited state. Men make two contracts — one forming civil society, another forming a government by consent — and transfer only the powers to make, execute and adjudicate law. The state thus holds delegated (trust) power, not original power: a ‘night-watchman’ state whose ‘sole purpose is the protection of property’, with separation of powers (legislative supreme, executive, federative) and a right of revolution against a government that betrays its trust.

Property and toleration. By the labour theory, ‘property is the product of one’s labour’, subject to limits (no spoilage, enough left for others). His Letter Concerning Toleration defends freedom of conscience — though, notably, not for atheists.

Hobbes vs Locke. Both use contract, but from opposite premises: Hobbes — a war-like state of nature, single contract, no natural rights retained, an absolute sovereign, ‘liberty where the law is silent’; Locke — a peaceful state of nature, two contracts, inalienable natural rights, a limited state, ‘no law, no liberty’.

Conclusion. Where Hobbes legitimizes state authority as absolute (to escape chaos), Locke legitimizes it as limited and accountable (to secure pre-existing rights) — which is why Locke, the ‘individualist out and out’, founds the liberal-constitutional tradition that runs through to Rawls.







Q — Assess Mill’s harm principle and defence of free expression, his status as a ‘reluctant democrat’, and his case for the equality of women, within his revision of utilitarianism. (UPSC 2014/2018/2021)





Gist — the spine to recall





Mill revised utilitarianism by adding quality — ‘better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’.



His ‘harm principle’: the state may restrict a person only to prevent harm to others.



He fiercely defended free speech — ‘all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’.



A ‘reluctant democrat’, he feared the ‘tyranny of the majority’; and (with Harriet Taylor) he championed women’s equality.





Model Answer

Mill revised utilitarianism by adding a qualitative dimension — ‘it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied’ — rescuing it from Bentham’s ‘pig’s philosophy’.

Liberty and the harm principle. Mill gives liberty priority: ‘over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign’. His harm principle holds that ‘the sole end for which mankind is warranted in interfering with the liberty of a person is to prevent harm to others’ — distinguishing self-regarding from other-regarding action.

Free expression. ‘All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility’ — even one dissentient must be heard, for the silenced opinion may be true, or contain part of the truth; hence his defence of the ‘crank’ whose rare genius benefits mankind.

A reluctant democrat. C.L. Wayper calls Mill a ‘reluctant democrat’: fearing the tyranny of the majority (a danger Tocqueville had diagnosed in Democracy in America), Mill proposed safeguards — plural/weighted voting, proportional representation and a strong second chamber — favouring quality over mere numbers.

Subjection of women. In The Subjection of Women (influenced by Harriet Taylor), Mill attacked the legal subordination of women as ‘one of the chief hindrances to human improvement’ — ‘there remains no legal slave save the mistress of every house’ — and argued equality would end the family as ‘a school of despotism’ and ‘double the mass of mental faculties’; he supported women’s suffrage.

Conclusion. Mill is the ‘first serious liberal democrat’ (Macpherson) — balancing utility with liberty, majority rule with minority rights, and pioneering the case for women’s equality — even if Barker faults his self-/other-regarding distinction as a ‘prophet of empty liberty’.







Q — Discuss Marx’s base-superstructure model, class and class struggle, and alienation; and how Gramsci’s concepts of hegemony, the integral state and organic intellectuals rescued Marxism from economic determinism. (UPSC 2015/2016/2020 + Gramsci 2013/2016/2019)





Gist — the spine to recall





Marx: the economic ‘base’ (who owns production) shapes the whole ‘superstructure’ (law, politics, ideas).



History is class struggle; capitalism exploits via surplus value and alienates the worker from his work, product and self.



Gramsci asked why revolution failed — answer: the ruling class rules by ‘hegemony’ (consent), not just force.



So Gramsci gave the superstructure autonomy — rescuing Marxism from crude economic determinism.





Model Answer

For Marx, historical materialism holds that the economic base (mode of production) determines the superstructure: ‘in order to think we must live, to live we must eat, and to eat we must produce’. History advances through class conflict — ‘the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’ — across stages from slave to feudal to capitalist to communist.

Class, surplus value, alienation. Capitalism exploits the worker through surplus value (labour alone creates value; the capitalist pockets the unpaid surplus), and alienates him at four levels — from the process of production, the product, his social nature and himself. When the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows and the state ‘withers away’.

The problem. Marx’s prediction of revolution in advanced capitalist states failed — exposing the limits of treating the superstructure as a mere ‘reflection’ of the base (the charge of economic determinism).

Gramsci’s rescue. Gramsci, the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, gave it autonomy. The ruling class rules by hegemony — manufacturing consent through civil society (the consent-wing of the ‘integral state’, alongside coercive political society) so that the exploited accept their exploitation as ‘common sense’. Revolution therefore needs a war of position — an ideological battle led by organic intellectuals — before the ‘war of manoeuvre’.

Conclusion. Gramsci shifts the decisive struggle from economics to culture and consciousness, explaining capitalism’s durability and rescuing Marxism from determinism — the pivot from classical Marxism to the neo-Marxist analysis of ideology and hegemony.







Q — Critically examine Arendt’s conceptual triad of labour, work and action, her distinction between power and violence, and her conception of ‘the political’ as the antidote to totalitarianism. (UPSC 2019)





Gist — the spine to recall





Arendt splits human activity into labour (survival), work (making things) and action (public life among equals).



Action is the highest — it makes us truly human (‘zoon politikon’) through speech and plurality.



Power ≠ violence: power is people ‘acting in concert’; violence destroys power but can never create it.



Genuine political action and participation are the antidote to totalitarianism (and to the ‘banality of evil’).





Model Answer

In The Human Condition, Arendt distinguishes the vita activa into three: Labour (the animal laborans — biological necessity, where man is unfree), Work (the homo faber — making durable things), and Action (the highest — public interaction among equals).

Only action, with its two components freedom and plurality, makes man a zoon politikon: through speech and deed among others we disclose who we are and begin something new (‘natality’). Modernity inverts this — the ‘victory of animal laborans over zoon politikon’, the ‘rise of the social’ and ‘world alienation’ — crowding out genuine action.

Power vs violence. ‘Power corresponds to the human ability not just to act but to act in concert’; it ‘belongs to a group and exists only so long as the group holds together’. It is sharply distinct from violence: ‘where genuine power is absent, violence may emerge to fill the gap’, and ‘violence can destroy power but is utterly incapable of creating it’.

The political as antidote to totalitarianism. Totalitarianism (ideology + terror) destroys the plural public realm and reduces men to isolated, thoughtless functionaries — hence the banality of evil (Eichmann in Jerusalem): evil done ‘because of the absence of sound thinking and judgment’. The remedy is a revival of civic republicanism — active participation in a genuine political public sphere.

Conclusion. Arendt relocates freedom from the private/economic realm to the public realm of action, making participation the essence of politics and the safeguard against totalitarianism. Critics (Benhabib, feminists, Marxists) fault her rigid public/private divide for delegitimising material and economic justice — yet her warning that thoughtlessness enables evil remains profound.

Right = originally anti-statist;  a modern concept replacing the divine right of kings. Green : moral rights from reason/moral personality;  Salmond : legal right = ‘interest protected by rule of law’. Parekh : multiculturalism = ‘creative interplay’; universal principles via dialogue among civilisations. Susan Moller Okin : ‘multiculturalism is bad for women’;  Isaiah Berlin : value pluralism (incommensurable values). Universality (MQ3):  UDHR; universalism (Locke+Kant) vs cultural relativism (Boas, Asian values); Berlin’s value pluralism; dialogue not imposition. Q — “Good governance is achievable only by strengthening grass-root democracy.” Discuss participatory democracy, the global democratic deficit, and why democracy survived in India. Gist — the spine to recall Grass-root (participatory) democracy brings power close to people — the basis of good governance and inclusive development. Rousseau is its pioneer: ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’; participation is a precondition for freedom. Globally there is a ‘democratic deficit’ — Held’s ‘cosmopolitan democracy’ seeks to fix it. India’s democracy survived due to the freedom movement, elite commitment (Nehru), British institutions and its argumentative tradition. Model Answer Good governance — accountable, participatory, inclusive rule — depends on deepening democracy at the base.  Participatory democracy  brings decision-making close to citizens;  Rousseau , its pioneer, held that ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’ and that participation is ‘a precondition for freedom’. Forms and benefits.  It takes  institutionalised  forms (Panchayati Raj, RTI, citizen charters, the right to recall) and  non-institutionalised  forms (social movements).  Carole Pateman  identifies three benefits — it is ‘educative’ for citizens, realises the general will, and makes democracy inclusive — while  Elinor Ostrom  shows communities can sustainably manage common resources. The global democratic deficit.  Democracy has spread among states, but the  world order  has not become more democratic —  Stiglitz  notes the ‘democratic deficit’ of global institutions.  David Held’s   cosmopolitan model of democracy  proposes reforming the UN Security Council, IMF and World Bank, regional parliaments, and even global referenda to close the gap. Why democracy survived in India  (against the third-world trend): the elite’s commitment (Nehru’s faith in democracy), the legacy of the national movement and of British parliamentary institutions, India’s  argumentative tradition  (Sen), enabling constitutional provisions (a free press, independent judiciary and Election Commission), its very size and diversity, and the strict separation of civil and military authority. Conclusion.  Good governance is ultimately ‘bottom-up’: strengthening grass-root democracy makes government responsive and legitimate, while reforming global institutions extends the same democratic logic beyond the nation-state — exactly the direction India’s resilient democracy points toward. Plato  decried democracy;  Aristotle : a ‘perverted’ form, prefers a mixed constitution. Classical (normative):  protective (Locke/Bentham) + developmental (Mill/Green/Laski) models. Modern (empirical):  elitist (Pareto circulation of elites; Michels iron law of oligarchy) + pluralist. Schumpeter : democracy = ‘competitive struggle for the people’s vote’;  Dahl : ‘polyarchy’. Macpherson : ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’ reduces democracy to a ‘market equilibrium system’; developmental vs extractive power. Procedural  (institutions) vs  substantive  (equal, engaged citizens; welfare) democracy. Representation:  delegate model (Locke/Bentham) vs trustee model (Burke, Mill). Rousseau : ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’; ‘English free only once in five years’ — pioneer of participatory democracy. Habermas : ideal speech situation + communicative action + public sphere; ‘force of the better argument’. Joshua Cohen : features of deliberative democracy;  Nancy Fraser : ‘counter-public’. Carole Pateman : participation is educative, realises general will, makes democracy inclusive. Lee thesis  (Lee Kuan Yew): democracy slows development, a ‘Western obsession’;  Sen : development as freedom; free press prevents famine. Sen’s 3 values:  intrinsic, institutional, educational. David Held : cosmopolitan model of democracy for the global democratic deficit;  Huntington : three waves of democratisation. Why India’s democracy survived:  elite commitment, national movement, British institutions, argumentative tradition, diversity, civil-military separation. Macpherson (M2):  democracy = humanist empowerment; developmental vs extractive power; social ownership + liberal institutions; Norman Barry’s critique. Three models (M3):  representative (delegate/trustee; tyranny of majority) → participative (Rousseau/Pateman) → deliberative. Deliberative (M4):  Habermas ideal speech + public sphere; Cohen features; Fraser counter-public; voice over choice; Waldron vs Dworkin. Participation + deliberation (M5):  participation = base (Arendt), deliberation = quality (Habermas); each incomplete without the other. Democracy-development (M6):  Lee thesis (authoritarian growth) vs Sen (development as freedom; famine argument; 3 values); Asian values. Grass-root + global (M7):  participatory democracy (Rousseau/Pateman/Ostrom); Held’s cosmopolitan model; why India’s democracy survived. His answer rescued Marxism from ‘crude economic determinism’ by giving the  superstructure  real autonomy — he is the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’. Hegemony.  The ruling class rules not by force alone but by  consent . Hegemony is ‘the ability of the ruling class to make its values live in the minds of the subaltern classes as their own common sense’ — ‘a kind of exploitation in which the exploited find happiness in their exploitation’. It ‘cannot be taken for granted; it must be produced continuously’. Political vs civil society.  The  integral state  =  political society  (the coercive apparatus — government, police, courts) +  civil society  (the consent-manufacturing institutions — family, school, church, media). Civil society is the ‘first layer of protection’, a ‘shock absorber’; where it is strong (an ‘opaque state’) exploitation is hidden and revolution hard, unlike a ‘transparent state’. Intellectuals.  ‘All men are intellectuals, but not all have the social function of intellectuals.’  Organic intellectuals  rise with a class (managers, engineers, civil servants) and can build  counter-hegemony ;  traditional intellectuals  (e.g. the clergy) appear class-neutral while maintaining continuity. Two-stage revolution.  Change requires first a  war of position  — an  ideological  struggle fought ‘at the level of the mind’, in which organic intellectuals form a  historic bloc  and build counter-hegemony — followed by the  war of manoeuvre , the physical seizure of power ‘once the mind is shaped’.  Bipin Chandra  cites the Indian national movement as the classic example. Critique & significance.  Althusser  faults him for slighting the coercive apparatus;  Perry Anderson  that ‘civil society’ pulls him from Marxism. Yet by locating power in culture and consent, Gramsci reshaped Marxism and inspired the Frankfurt School — showing that the decisive battle is often fought over ideas, not arms. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Lasswell & Kaplan : politics = ‘the shaping and sharing of power’;  Russell : power = ‘production of intended effects’. Hannah Arendt : power is ‘acting in concert’, ‘belongs to a group’; ‘violence can destroy power but never create it’. Steven Lukes : 3 faces — decision-making, agenda-setting, thought-control. Forms of power:  political, economic, ideological (‘ruling ideas = ideas of ruling class’ — Marx & Engels). Elitists:  Pareto  (circulation of elites),  Michels  (iron law of oligarchy),  Mills  (power elite). Pluralist:  Dahl  (polyarchy, ‘honest broker’);  Foucault:  ‘power is everywhere’, productive, power/knowledge, Panopticon. Authority = Power + Legitimacy;  ‘naked sword’ vs ‘sword in scabbard’. Weber : 3 legitimate authorities — traditional, charismatic, rational-legal. David Beetham : legitimacy = rules + shared belief + expressed consent;  Tom Tyler : procedure matters most. Habermas ,  Legitimation Crisis : democracy’s welfare demands vs capitalism’s profit needs;  Anthony King : ‘government overload’. Marx : ideology = false consciousness;  Mannheim : ideology vs utopia;  Destutt de Tracy  coined ‘ideology’. Daniel Bell : ‘end of ideology’;  Fukuyama : ‘end of history’;  Huntington : clash of civilizations. Gramsci : hegemony = rule by consent; integral state = political + civil society. Intellectuals:  organic (rise with a class → counter-hegemony) vs traditional (appear neutral). Revolution:  war of position (ideological) → war of manoeuvre (physical); historic bloc; Indian national movement (Bipin Chandra). Gramsci critics:  Althusser  (ignores coercion),  Perry Anderson  (civil society pulls him from Marxism). Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Power (M1):  conventional = domination (Russell/Dahl) vs constructive = ‘acting in concert’ (Arendt); Lukes’ 3 faces; political/economic/ideological forms. Theories (M2):  elitist (Pareto/Michels/Mills) vs pluralist (Dahl polyarchy) vs Marxist (economic) vs feminist (patriarchy) vs Foucault (productive, everywhere). Power vs authority (M3):  authority = power + legitimacy; Weber’s 3 types (traditional/charismatic/rational-legal); Beetham’s 3 principles. Legitimation crisis (M4):  Habermas — democracy’s welfare demands vs capitalism’s profit; ‘government overload’; elections as safety valve. Ideology & the two ‘ends’ (M5):  ideology = false consciousness (Marx); end of ideology (Bell) & end of history (Fukuyama) vs Huntington. Gramsci (M6):  hegemony = rule by consent; political vs civil society; organic vs traditional intellectuals; war of position → war of manoeuvre. Killer quotes:  Arendt — ‘violence can destroy power but never create it’; Foucault — ‘power is everywhere’; Gramsci — the exploited ‘find happiness in their exploitation’; Marx — ‘ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class’. Model Answer Liberalism is a  meta-ideology  built on a commitment to the individual, with five core values —  individualism, freedom, reason, justice and toleration . It was  revolutionary  in its day: by grounding legitimate rule in the  consent of the people , it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings. Classical liberalism  ( Locke  — ‘father of classical liberalism’,  Adam Smith, Herbert Spencer ) champions a minimal ‘night-watchman’ state, laissez-faire, natural rights and  negative liberty ;  Jefferson : ‘that government is best which governs least’.  Macpherson  labels its individual ‘possessive’. Modern / positive liberalism  ( T.H. Green, Hobhouse, Laski ) makes the state a ‘source of virtue’ enabling  positive liberty : Green — ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’, the state ‘hinders the hindrances’ to self-development, justifying the welfare state. Neo-liberalism  ( Hayek, Nozick, Friedman ) reverses this — ‘rolling back the state’ and ‘market fundamentalism’.  Hayek : ‘planning is the road to serfdom’, ‘social justice is a mirage’;  Friedman : freedom is possible only through the market. It became the ideology of globalization — Thatcherism/Reaganism, shock therapy, the WTO (1995) and the  Washington Consensus . Conclusion. Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017) Gist — the spine to recall Postmodernism distrusts all ‘grand theories’ (like Marxism or liberalism) that claim one universal truth. Lyotard: postmodernism = ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’; there are many truths, not one. ‘End of ideology’ (Bell): after WWII the big ideological battles died down in a welfare-capitalist consensus. ‘End of history’ (Fukuyama): after the Cold War, liberal democracy won — but both theses were overtaken by new conflicts. Model Answer Postmodernism is a rejection of Modernism that ‘emphasises the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’;  Nietzsche  is regarded as its father (‘God is dead’, ‘will to power’).  Jean-Francois Lyotard  gave its defining formula: postmodernism is  ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’  — disbelief in any grand, universal theory, for ‘there is not one but many truths’. Its key moves:  Foucault’s  ‘power/knowledge’ (‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’);  Derrida’s   deconstruction  of the ‘metaphysics of presence’; and  Baudrillard’s  ‘hyper-reality’ where media becomes more real than reality. End of ideology.  Daniel Bell  (with  Lipset, Dahrendorf ) argued that after the Second World War the great ideological conflicts had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus. Critics ( Macpherson, MacIntyre ) replied that ‘the end of ideology is itself an ideology’. End of history.  Francis Fukuyama  extended this after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over all rivals (a Hegelian idea).  Samuel Huntington  countered with the ‘clash of civilizations’ — ethnic and religious identity, not ideology, would drive future conflict. Conclusion.  All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ to universal truth or ideological struggle, yet the persistence of nationalism, religion and inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives, but its own relativism risks leaving no ground on which to criticise injustice. Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014) Gist — the spine to recall Socialism’s core value is social/economic equality and cooperation over competition. Revolutionary socialism (Marx): overthrow capitalism in one stroke; Evolutionary socialism: reach it gradually through the ballot and reform. Pre-Marx ‘utopian’ socialists (Owen, Fourier, Saint-Simon) dreamed of ideal communities but had no scientific programme. Today socialism revives as anti-capitalism (Occupy, inequality debates) — ‘socialism or barbarism’ (Wallerstein). Model Answer Socialism is defined by its opposition to capitalism; its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and cooperation over competition.  C.E.M. Joad  quipped that ‘socialism is like a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’. Pre-Marxist / utopian socialism.  Robert Owen  (who first used ‘socialist’) proposed ‘villages of cooperation’;  Charles Fourier  wanted to make work pleasant;  Saint-Simon  favoured rule by scientific ‘luminaries’. Marx called them  ‘utopian’  because they painted ideal futures without a scientific analysis of capitalism or a programme to get there. Revolutionary vs evolutionary.  Revolutionary socialism  (the Marxist tradition) seeks to overthrow capitalism ‘in a single stroke’ for a classless society.  Evolutionary socialism  (the liberal/‘democratic socialist’ tradition) proceeds gradually and parliamentarily:  revisionism  ( Bernstein  — workers with the vote need no revolution),  Fabianism  ( G.B. Shaw, the Webbs ; inspiration for Nehruvian socialism),  syndicalism  and  guild socialism  ( G.D.H. Cole ). Rebirth as anti-capitalism.  With inequality rising, socialism revives as an anti-capitalist critique —  Ralph Miliband’s   Socialism for a Sceptical Age , movements like Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and  Wallerstein’s  stark choice, ‘socialism or barbarism’. Conclusion.  Evolutionary socialism made socialism democratically respectable but is charged with legitimising the bourgeois state (a ‘safety valve’); its 21st-century relevance lies less in seizing power than in supplying the moral vocabulary of the fight against inequality — socialism reborn as anti-capitalism. Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Marxism is the ‘scientific’ theory of socialism: history is driven by class conflict over who owns production. Dialectical materialism: reality is matter in conflict (thesis-antithesis-synthesis); historical materialism: the economic ‘base’ shapes the ‘superstructure’. Class struggle drives history; capitalism exploits workers by pocketing ‘surplus value’. Relevance: inequality, 2008 crisis and Occupy revive it (Piketty, Eagleton) — though its predictions largely failed. Model Answer Marxism, founded by  Marx  and  Engels , claims to give socialism a ‘scientific’ basis, treating history as the conflict of antagonistic classes. Dialectical materialism  fuses  Hegel’s  dialectic (thesis–antithesis–synthesis) with materialism — matter, not idea, is the essence of reality;  Engels  gives its three laws.  Historical materialism  applies this to society: the economic  base  (mode of production) determines the  superstructure  (law, politics, ideas), driving history through stages — slave → feudal → capitalist → socialist → communist. Class struggle and surplus value.  ‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’; the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’. Capitalism exploits workers through  surplus value  — labour alone creates value, but the capitalist pockets the unpaid surplus. When the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows. Contemporary relevance.  Marxism’s predictions (imminent revolution, immiseration) largely failed, and state-socialist regimes collapsed. Yet its  critique of capitalism  endures:  Thomas Piketty  ( Capital in the Twenty-First Century ) documents widening inequality,  Terry Eagleton  ( Why Marx Was Right ) defends its core, and movements like Occupy Wall Street echo its concerns. Conclusion.  As a blueprint for revolution Marxism has been largely discredited; as a  diagnostic tool  for exploitation, alienation and inequality under capitalism it remains strikingly relevant — which is why each crisis of capitalism renews interest in Marx. Q — How did neo-Marxism (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) reformulate the base–superstructure relationship? Gist — the spine to recall Classical Marxism said the economy (base) simply determines everything else (superstructure). Neo-Marxists said culture and ideas have their own power — that’s why workers didn’t revolt. Gramsci: the ruling class rules by ‘hegemony’ (consent), so revolution needs a ‘war of position’ in the realm of ideas. Frankfurt School (Marcuse’s ‘one-dimensional man’) and Althusser (ideological state apparatuses) deepened this cultural turn. Model Answer Classical Marxism treated the  superstructure  (ideas, law, culture, the state) as a mere reflection of the economic  base . When revolution failed to arrive in the advanced West,  neo-Marxists  rescued Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’ by giving the superstructure real autonomy. Antonio Gramsci , the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, argued the ruling class rules not just by coercion but by  hegemony  — manufacturing consent through  civil society  (school, church, media), so the exploited accept their exploitation as ‘common sense’. Revolution therefore needs first a  war of position  — an ideological struggle led by  organic intellectuals  to build counter-hegemony — before the physical ‘war of manoeuvre’. The  Frankfurt School  ( Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse ) developed  critical theory  and the idea of the ‘culture industry’;  Marcuse’s   One-Dimensional Man  shows how capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ that absorb dissent. Louis Althusser  (the structuralist school) added the  ‘ideological state apparatuses’  and  interpellation  (ideology ‘hails’ individuals into subjects), and a ‘multi-sectoral’ analysis rejecting economic determinism — the base is determinant only ‘in the last instance’. Conclusion.  Neo-Marxism shifted the decisive battleground from the  economy to culture and consciousness  — explaining capitalism’s durability and reshaping Marxism into a theory of ideology and hegemony rather than of inevitable economic collapse. Q — Why is the sex/gender distinction central to feminist analysis? Distinguish liberal, socialist and radical feminism and the waves of feminism. (UPSC 2012/2019) Gist — the spine to recall Sex is biological (unchangeable); gender is the social role ‘made’ by society (changeable) — so women’s subordination is not natural. This lets feminists reject ‘biology is destiny’ and demand change. Liberal feminism = equal rights within the system; socialist = link patriarchy to capitalism; radical = patriarchy is the deepest oppression. Three waves: 1st = suffrage/legal rights; 2nd = ‘women’s liberation’/private sphere; 3rd = difference and diversity. Model Answer Feminist ideology rests on two beliefs — ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. The  sex/gender distinction  is central because  sex  is biological and fixed, whereas  gender  is a cultural construct that can be changed — as  Simone de Beauvoir  put it, ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’. This shatters the claim that ‘biology is destiny’ and makes subordination a social wrong to be corrected. Liberal feminism  ( Mary Wollstonecraft ,  A Vindication of the Rights of Woman ;  J.S. Mill ;  Betty Friedan ) is reformist — it seeks equal legal and political rights within the existing system, arguing gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’. Socialist feminism  ( Engels ,  The Origin of the Family ;  Juliet Mitchell ) links patriarchy to  capitalism  — women are a ‘reserve army of labour’ whose unpaid domestic work reproduces labour power.  Radical feminism  ( Kate Millett, Germaine Greer, Beauvoir ) locates the root in  patriarchy  itself — ‘the personal is political’ — reaching into family and sexuality. The three waves.  The  first wave  (to the 1960s) won legal and voting rights (suffrage); the  second wave  (1961–91) was the ‘women’s liberation’ movement targeting the private sphere ( Friedan’s  ‘problem with no name’); the  third wave  (from the 1990s) embraced the politics of difference — black, postcolonial and eco-feminism. Conclusion.  The sex/gender distinction is the theoretical foundation of all feminism because it turns women’s subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice — though the strands differ on whether the cure is equal rights, the end of capitalism, or the overthrow of patriarchy. Q — “One is not born, but becomes, a woman.” Examine radical feminism and patriarchy, and evaluate eco-feminism and the newer strands (black, postcolonial). (UPSC 2017) Gist — the spine to recall Radical feminism says patriarchy — male domination — is the oldest and deepest form of oppression, rooted in the family and sexuality. It coined ‘the personal is political’: private life (marriage, sex, housework) is a site of power. Eco-feminism links the domination of women with the domination of nature (Vandana Shiva). Newer strands (black, postcolonial) say mainstream feminism ignored race and class — not all women are the same. Model Answer Radical feminism, the defining strand of the  second wave , holds that  patriarchy  — ‘rule by men’ — is the most fundamental and universal form of oppression, prior to class or race.  Kate Millett  defines it as a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’. Its rallying idea is  ‘the personal is political’ : the private sphere of family, marriage and sexuality is itself a structure of power.  Susan Brownmiller  (‘rape is an institution of patriarchy’) and  Simone de Beauvoir  ( The Second Sex , ‘woman is made, not born’) show how women are constructed as the  ‘Other’ ; some radicals advocate androgyny as the escape. Eco-feminism  (a term credited to  Francoise d’Eaubonne ; developed by  Vandana Shiva  and  Mary Daly ) links the  domination of women  with the  domination of nature  — both treated as passive resources by a masculinist, exploitative order — so women are natural allies of ecology. Newer strands.  Black feminism  ( bell hooks ) and  postcolonial feminism  ( Chandra Talpade Mohanty ) charge that mainstream (white, middle-class) feminism universalised one experience and ignored  race and class ; the ‘third-world woman’ cannot be spoken for by Western feminists. Conclusion.  Radical feminism transformed feminism by politicising the private sphere, but its assumption of a single ‘women’s experience’ — an ‘essential’ femininity — is exactly what eco-, black and postcolonial feminists contest, moving feminism from sisterhood-as-sameness to a  politics of difference . Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon. Gist — the spine to recall Fascism glorifies the nation/state and the leader above the individual — ‘the individual is nothing’. It is anti-rational: it exalts will, struggle, war and myth over reason (‘1789 is dead’). Core tenets: struggle/social Darwinism, leader-worship, ultranationalism, totalitarian corporatist state. It is not a coherent doctrine (a ‘hodge-podge’); Marxists (Laski) call it ‘capitalism defending itself’. Model Answer Fascism (from  fasces , ‘strength through unity’) subordinates the individual utterly to the nation and state — ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’ — aiming to forge a ‘new man’. Because it lacks a systematic doctrine it is often called a ‘ hodge-podge of ideologies ’ or a ‘political religion’ rather than a coherent ideology. Anti-rationalism  is its hallmark: a counter-Enlightenment cult of  will, instinct and myth  over reason —  Sorel’s  ‘political myths’, Mussolini’s ‘action not talk’, ‘1789 is dead’. Its other core tenets:  struggle  (social Darwinism — ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’);  leadership and elitism  (the Führerprinzip, Nietzsche’s Übermensch); ‘national socialism’; and chauvinistic  ultranationalism . The state.  Fascism is  totalitarian  and  corporatist  — for  Mussolini  and  Gentile , ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’, drawing on Hegel’s worship of the state. Nazism added  racialism  — Aryan supremacy, anti-Semitism and the ‘final solution’. Merely inter-war?  Ernst Nolte  sees fascism as a product of specific  inter-war circumstances  (defeat, depression, fear of communism), whereas  Erich Fromm  roots it in human nature itself — the ‘fear of freedom’ — implying it can recur.  Laski  (Marxist) calls it ‘a desperate attempt by capitalism to protect itself’. Conclusion.  Fascism is best seen not as a coherent ideology but as a reactive, anti-rational movement of extreme nationalism and leader-worship. Fromm’s ‘fear of freedom’ warns that it was not merely an inter-war accident — its impulses resurface wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Liberalism = meta-ideology;  core values: individualism, freedom, reason, justice, toleration. Liberal phases:  classical (Locke/Smith, night-watchman) → modern (Green, positive liberty) → neo-liberal (Hayek/Nozick/Friedman). Green : ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’; state ‘hinders the hindrances’. Lyotard : postmodernism = ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’;  Nietzsche  = father of postmodernism. Bell : ‘end of ideology’;  Fukuyama : ‘end of history’;  Huntington : clash of civilizations. Socialism:  Joad — ‘a hat that has lost its shape’; core value = social equality. Utopian socialists:  Owen  (villages of cooperation),  Fourier ,  Saint-Simon . Evolutionary socialism:  revisionism (Bernstein), Fabianism (Shaw/Webbs), syndicalism, guild socialism (Cole). Marxism:  dialectical + historical materialism; base→superstructure; class struggle; surplus value. Marx : ‘history of all society is the history of class struggle’; ‘workers have nothing to lose but their chains’. Neo-Marxism:  Gramsci  (hegemony, war of position), Frankfurt School (Marcuse ‘one-dimensional man’), Althusser (ISAs, interpellation). Feminism:  sex (biological) vs gender (social); Beauvoir — ‘one is not born but becomes a woman’. Feminist strands:  liberal (Wollstonecraft/Mill), socialist (Engels), radical (Millett/Greer); eco-feminism (d’Eaubonne, Shiva). Waves:  1st suffrage; 2nd women’s liberation (Friedan’s ‘problem with no name’); 3rd difference (black/postcolonial). Fascism:  fasces = strength through unity; anti-rationalism; ‘1789 is dead’; totalitarian corporatist state. Laski : fascism = ‘capitalism defending itself’;  Fromm : ‘fear of freedom’;  Nolte : inter-war product. Last-Minute Revision Sheet (1 page) Liberalism (MQ1):  revolutionary (vs feudalism); classical→modern→neo-liberal; neo-liberalism = globalization’s ideology; social-liberal revival. Postmodernism/ends (MQ2):  Lyotard ‘incredulity to metanarratives’; Bell (end of ideology), Fukuyama (end of history) vs Huntington. Socialism (MQ3):  utopian (Owen/Fourier/Saint-Simon); revolutionary vs evolutionary (Bernstein/Fabians); reborn as anti-capitalism. Marxism (MQ4):  dialectical+historical materialism; class struggle; surplus value; relevance (Piketty, Eagleton) despite failed predictions. Neo-Marxism (MQ5):  Gramsci hegemony/war of position; Frankfurt School culture industry; Althusser ISAs — culture over economy. Feminism (MQ6):  sex vs gender; liberal/socialist/radical; three waves (suffrage/liberation/difference). Radical & new feminism (MQ7):  patriarchy, personal is political, Beauvoir ‘Other’; eco-feminism (Shiva); black/postcolonial critique. Fascism (MQ8):  individual = nothing; anti-rationalism, struggle, leader, corporatist state; Nolte vs Fromm; Laski’s Marxist critique. Killer quotes:  Beauvoir — ‘one is not born but becomes a woman’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’; Mussolini — ‘nothing beyond the State’; Marx — ‘nothing to lose but chains’. content.text: Syllabus — Indian Political Thought: Dharmashastra, Arthashastra and Buddhist traditions; Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar, M.N. Roy. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 9)

the ancient traditions — Dharmashastra (Manu), Arthashastra (Kautilya) and Buddhist political thought — and the modern thinkers Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar and M.N. Roy.

Manu (dharma, varna), Kautilya (Saptanga, Mandala, Danda-niti, Matsyanyaya), Buddha (MahaSammat, Dhamma), Sir Syed (two-nation theory), Aurobindo (spiritual nationalism, Purna Swaraj), Gandhi (Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya, Trusteeship), Ambedkar (annihilation of caste, social democracy), M.N. Q — Explicate the ideological components of Gandhism — Truth/Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship — and evaluate his critique of modern Western civilization and his view of the state. (UPSC 2020/2019/2016/2015)
Gandhism is Gandhi’s practical philosophy — he called himself not a philosopher but a ‘strategist’.
Its core: Truth + Non-violence → Satyagraha (‘soul-force’, self-suffering against evil, not the evil-doer).
Swaraj = self-rule/self-control (→ Ram Rajya, a near-stateless society); Sarvodaya/Trusteeship = the rich hold wealth in trust for all.
He attacked modern Western civilization as ‘satanic’/materialist and saw the state as a ‘soulless machine’ based on force.

Gandhism fuses ethics and politics through the ‘continuity of ends and means’ — ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’. Though Trusteeship and Ram Rajya are criticised as impractical, Gandhi’s non-violent Satyagraha remains his enduring contribution to world politics.
Q — Explain the sources and salient features of ancient Indian political thought, and examine the significance of Dharma in the Dharmashastra (Manu) tradition. (UPSC 2020)

It treats Dharma (moral law) and Danda (political power) together, in a continuum, not separately.
Manu, the ‘first law-giver’, is the chief exponent of the Dharmashastra tradition.
Dharma is central: it holds society together; the king is under Dharma (divine personality but NOT divine rights).

Q — Discuss Kautilya’s theory of statecraft — the Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti and the four Upayas — and his analysis of corruption. (UPSC 2017/2007)
Kautilya’s Arthashastra is a practical manual of administration and statecraft.
Saptanga = the 7 organs/elements of the state (king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army, ally) — an ‘organic’ theory.
Mandala Siddhanta = geopolitics of concentric friends and enemies; Shadgunya = six-fold foreign policy; four Upayas = Sama, Dama, Danda, Bheda.
On corruption: ‘inevitable yet undesirable’ — ‘forty ways of embezzlement’; hard to detect (‘fish drinking water’).

His remedies: frequent transfers, protection of whistle-blowers, rewards for the honest and punishment of ‘the entire chain’.

Q — Draw parallels and contrasts between Kautilya’s Arthashastra and the realist tradition of Machiavelli, and compare Dharmashastra and Arthashastra with reference to state power. (UPSC 2012/2010)
Both Kautilya and Machiavelli are realists who let the ruler use any means for the state’s survival and expansion.
But Kautilya’s king stays UNDER dharma, while Machiavelli’s prince is above religion/ethics.
Kautilya predates Machiavelli by ~1800 years — so calling him the ‘Indian Machiavelli’ is chronologically backwards.
Dharmashastra puts moral law (dharma) above power; Arthashastra puts power (danda) above morality.

Q — Examine the salient features of Buddhist political thought, assess whether it gave a greater ethical foundation to ancient Indian thought, and compare it with the Hindu tradition. (UPSC 2021)
Buddhism is called the ‘rebel child of Hinduism’ — egalitarian, rational and republican.
Its state arises from human corruption, and its king is ELECTED (MahaSammat) — an early social contract and ‘primus inter pares’.
It rules by Dhamma (ethical persuasion), not force; the Chakravartin ‘wins hearts’ rather than land.
So it gives a stronger ETHICAL, deliberative and anti-caste foundation than the hierarchical Hindu tradition.

Q — Assess Sir Syed Ahmed Khan as a social reformer and modernizer, tracing his transition from champion of Hindu-Muslim unity to originator of the two-nation theory. (UPSC 2021/2013)
Sir Syed believed Muslims could rise only by modernizing — embracing science and English education.
As a reformer he founded MAO College (later Aligarh Muslim University) and opposed purdah, polygamy and irrationalism.
Phase 1: he preached Hindu-Muslim unity — the ‘two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’.
Phase 2: fearing Hindu-majority domination in elections, he opposed representative government and became the originator of the two-nation theory.

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan held that Muslim upliftment was ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, which he saw as ‘most compatible with science and rationality’ — ‘the Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’.

(which became Aligarh Muslim University). A ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’, he attacked religious intolerance and denounced ‘purdah, polygamy and easy divorce’. His status among Muslims is compared to Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s among Hindus.

Initially he stressed a common Indian nationhood: Hindus and Muslims are ‘the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’, sharing ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’. By ‘qaum’ he meant ‘both Hindus and Muslims’, and he worked with Hindu leaders.

Sir Syed was a genuine modernizer who dragged a conservative community toward science and education, but his later communal politics laid the ideological seed of Partition — a reformer whose educational legacy and political legacy pull in opposite directions.
Q — Analyse Sri Aurobindo’s theory of cultural/spiritual nationalism, his conception of Swaraj and his idea of freedom. (UPSC 2017/2016/2014/2013)
Aurobindo fused nationalism with spirituality — India is not just a land but a living Mother with a divine mission.
‘Nationalism is not a mere political programme but a way of life like religion.’
He was the first to define Swaraj as complete independence (Purna Swaraj), a precondition for India’s spiritual destiny.
Real freedom for him is ‘inner freedom’ — not just political liberty but self-realisation.

Sri Aurobindo ‘connected nationalism with spirituality’; Romain Rolland saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’. In his extremist phase he rejected the Moderates’ constitutionalism and pioneered a theory of
that prepared the ground for Gandhi.
Applying the German (Herder) idea that ‘the nation is natural and has a spirit’, and inspired by Bankim’s vision of
and Vivekananda’s Neo-Vedanta, Aurobindo held: ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the
nation is a faith, the nation is a religion, the nation has a spirit
’. India has a ‘divine mission’ to give spirituality to the world.
He was the first to interpret Swaraj as

— complete independence — pursued through swadeshi, boycott and national education. ‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’; to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’ — Swaraj is the ‘necessary condition for India to accomplish its destined goal’.
He found the liberal (anarchic) view ‘mechanical’ and the socialist view neglectful of the individual; real freedom is
— ‘obeying the law of our own existence’ (swadharma). His later thought turned to
Sacchidananda, the Supermind and Integral Yoga
, making national self-realisation a stage toward humanity’s spiritual evolution.

Aurobindo raised nationalism from a political programme to a spiritual vocation. Critics call his spiritual nationalism reactionary and idealistic, yet by rooting freedom in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma and insisting on Purna Swaraj, he decisively radicalised the Indian freedom movement.

Q — Evaluate Ambedkar’s idea of social justice — annihilation of caste, critique of Hinduism and of Marxism, and his conception of social/economic/political democracy — comparing his egalitarian justice with Rawls. (UPSC 2022/2020/2018/2016/2013)
Ambedkar’s central mission was the ‘annihilation of caste’ — caste is not division of labour but ‘division of labourers’.
He held Hinduism = Brahmanism, sanctified by texts like Manusmriti, so he finally converted to Buddhism.
He demanded social + economic democracy, not just political — ‘political democracy cannot last without social democracy’.
His justice is egalitarian/outcome-focused (uplift the depressed), going beyond Rawls’ procedural ‘justice as fairness’.
Ambedkar, ‘chief architect of the Constitution’ and himself born a Mahar, made the
his central concern. Caste, he argued in

‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, sanctified by the Vedas and Manusmriti (on which he would ‘put dynamite’); finding no reform possible from within, he
(1956) — ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.
For Ambedkar democracy is ‘a way of life’ resting on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’. He insisted on completing
political democracy with social and economic democracy
: ‘we must make our political democracy a social democracy as well; political democracy cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy’ — secured through

He rejected two Marxist claims: that religion is mere ‘opium’ (Buddhism, based on karuna, samata and prajna, is not), and that the state is the chief oppressor — for Ambedkar ‘society is more exploitative than the state’, so the state must be an instrument of emancipation.
