contentText: Syllabus — Indian Political Thought: Dharmashastra, Arthashastra and Buddhist traditions; Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar, M.N. Roy. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 9) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the ancient traditions — Dharmashastra (Manu), Arthashastra (Kautilya) and Buddhist political thought — and the modern thinkers Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar and M.N. Roy. Must-know thinkers & concepts:  Manu (dharma, varna), Kautilya (Saptanga, Mandala, Danda-niti, Matsyanyaya), Buddha (MahaSammat, Dhamma), Sir Syed (two-nation theory), Aurobindo (spiritual nationalism, Purna Swaraj), Gandhi (Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya, Trusteeship), Ambedkar (annihilation of caste, social democracy), M.N. Roy (radical humanism). PYQ trend:  Gandhi (2020/2019/2016/2015) and Ambedkar (2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) are the highest-yield; also Kautilya’s statecraft (2017/2012/2010/2007), Buddhist ethics (2021), Aurobindo (2017/2016/2014/2013), Sir Syed (2021/2013), Dharma (2020), M.N. Roy. Master Questions Q — Explicate the ideological components of Gandhism — Truth/Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship — and evaluate his critique of modern Western civilization and his view of the state. (UPSC 2020/2019/2016/2015) Gist — the spine to recall Gandhism is Gandhi’s practical philosophy — he called himself not a philosopher but a ‘strategist’. Its core: Truth + Non-violence → Satyagraha (‘soul-force’, self-suffering against evil, not the evil-doer). Swaraj = self-rule/self-control (→ Ram Rajya, a near-stateless society); Sarvodaya/Trusteeship = the rich hold wealth in trust for all. He attacked modern Western civilization as ‘satanic’/materialist and saw the state as a ‘soulless machine’ based on force. Model Answer Gandhi denied there was any ‘Gandhism’;  Humayun Kabir  called him ‘not a philosopher but a strategist… a psychologist’. His ideas (in  Hind Swaraj  and  My Experiments with Truth , drawing on the Gita, Tolstoy and Ruskin) cohere around a few components. Truth and Non-violence.  ‘God and truth are inseparable’, and  Ahimsa  is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’. From these flows  Satyagraha  (satya + agraha) — ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, directed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’, and distinct from mere passive resistance.  Martin Luther King : ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’. Swaraj.  Gandhi’s idea of liberty means  self-rule and self-control  — political (Panchayati Raj →  Ram Rajya , a stateless society), economic, social and cultural. His famous image: ‘I do not want my house to be walled in… I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house… but I refuse to be blown off my feet’. Sarvodaya & Trusteeship.  From Ruskin’s  Unto This Last ,  Sarvodaya  = ‘the uplift of all’, resting on  bread labour  and  Trusteeship  — capitalists as ‘trustees, not owners’ (‘there is enough for need but not for greed’). Critique of modernity & the state.  In  Hind Swaraj  he condemns modern Western civilization as materialist and ‘satanic’, and sees the  state  as ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion that stunts self-reliance — an anarchist ideal of ‘enlightened anarchy’ built on ‘oceanic circles’. Conclusion.  Gandhism fuses ethics and politics through the ‘continuity of ends and means’ — ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’. Though Trusteeship and Ram Rajya are criticised as impractical, Gandhi’s non-violent Satyagraha remains his enduring contribution to world politics. Q — Explain the sources and salient features of ancient Indian political thought, and examine the significance of Dharma in the Dharmashastra (Manu) tradition. (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall Ancient Indian thought rests on ‘riti’ (cosmic order) — like the Western idea of natural law. It treats Dharma (moral law) and Danda (political power) together, in a continuum, not separately. Manu, the ‘first law-giver’, is the chief exponent of the Dharmashastra tradition. Dharma is central: it holds society together; the king is under Dharma (divine personality but NOT divine rights). Model Answer Ancient Indian (‘Hindu’) political thought derives from  riti  — the all-pervading cosmic order discoverable through spiritual experience, analogous to the Western concept of  natural law . Its sources are the  Vedic texts  — shrutis (Vedas) and smritis (notably the  Manusmriti ). Salient features.  It shows ‘enormous continuity’ of dharma and danda; it is  communitarian, pluralistic and cosmopolitan  ( Sant Tukaram : ‘the entire world is a family’); but it is ‘non-critical’, taking a regressive rather than progressive view of history. Dharma vs Danda.  ‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’, differing only in  degree  — Indian thought treats them not ‘in silos but in a continuum’. In the  Dharmashastra , dharma is core and danda peripheral. Manu and the significance of Dharma.  Manu , the ‘first law-giver’ (Manasputra of Brahma), is the chief exponent.  Dharma  — the moral/natural/social order — is central: ‘ Prithvim Dharma Dhritam ’ (dharma is that which holds life on earth); its absence brings  arajakta  (anarchy) and  Matsya Nyaya  (‘big fish eats small fish’). The king, though of ‘divine personality’, has  no divine rights  — he is bound by Raj Dharma and stands  under the law . Conclusion.  Dharma is the master concept of ancient Indian polity — it legitimises and simultaneously limits kingship. Yet the tradition’s endorsement of the varna hierarchy and unequal punishment (‘lower the varna, higher the punishment’) drew  Ambedkar’s  sharp critique, exposing the tension between order and equality at its heart. Q — Discuss Kautilya’s theory of statecraft — the Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti and the four Upayas — and his analysis of corruption. (UPSC 2017/2007) Gist — the spine to recall Kautilya’s Arthashastra is a practical manual of administration and statecraft. Saptanga = the 7 organs/elements of the state (king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army, ally) — an ‘organic’ theory. Mandala Siddhanta = geopolitics of concentric friends and enemies; Shadgunya = six-fold foreign policy; four Upayas = Sama, Dama, Danda, Bheda. On corruption: ‘inevitable yet undesirable’ — ‘forty ways of embezzlement’; hard to detect (‘fish drinking water’). Model Answer Kautilya’s  Arthashastra  is essentially ‘a book on the art of administration’ and the first Indian text of  statecraft  and geopolitics. He held that ‘in the happiness of the subjects lies the happiness of the king’, but pursued it through hard-headed realism. Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti).  The state is an organism of  seven elements :  Swami  (king, the ‘Nabhi’/centre),  Amatya  (ministers),  Janapada  (territory + population),  Durga  (fort),  Kosha  (treasury — ‘all undertakings depend upon Kosha’),  Danda/Bala  (army) and  Mitra  (ally). ‘One wheel alone does not turn the chariot’ — the elements work together. Foreign policy.  The  Mandala Siddhanta  maps concentric rings of natural enemies (Ari) and friends (Mitra) around the  vijigishu  (‘one who aspires to victory’), with buffer (Madhyama) and neutral (Udasina) states. The  Shadgunya-niti  (six-fold policy — Sandhi, Vigraha, Asana, Yana, Samshraya, Dvaidhibhava) and the four  Upayas  (Sama, Dama, Danda, Bheda) are his diplomatic toolkit. Corruption.  Kautilya thought corruption ‘inevitable yet not desirable’: ‘just as it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue, so it is impossible for one dealing with government funds not to taste the king’s wealth’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’ — he lists ‘forty ways of embezzlement’. His remedies: frequent transfers, protection of whistle-blowers, rewards for the honest and punishment of ‘the entire chain’. Conclusion.  Kautilya’s statecraft is remarkably systematic and practical — an ancient science of realpolitik, administration and geopolitics that anticipates modern theories of the state as an organism and of the  balance of power . Q — Draw parallels and contrasts between Kautilya’s Arthashastra and the realist tradition of Machiavelli, and compare Dharmashastra and Arthashastra with reference to state power. (UPSC 2012/2010) Gist — the spine to recall Both Kautilya and Machiavelli are realists who let the ruler use any means for the state’s survival and expansion. But Kautilya’s king stays UNDER dharma, while Machiavelli’s prince is above religion/ethics. Kautilya predates Machiavelli by ~1800 years — so calling him the ‘Indian Machiavelli’ is chronologically backwards. Dharmashastra puts moral law (dharma) above power; Arthashastra puts power (danda) above morality. Model Answer Nehru called Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’, but since the  Arthashastra  predates  The Prince  by roughly  1800 years ,  Upinder Singh  rightly notes it would be more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’. Parallels.  Both are  realists  writing for a motherland under threat, seeking consolidation; both permit the ruler ‘all sorts of means’ and support an imperialist foreign policy; both, in effect, hold that ‘the end justifies the means’.  Max Weber  judged that ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’. Contrasts.  The decisive difference is ethics: ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains  under dharma ’. Kautilya’s king is ‘generous and kind’ and treats power as a  means, not an end ; Machiavelli’s prince rules ‘with an iron hand’. Machiavelli gives generic advice, Kautilya precise administrative detail — and ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’. Dharmashastra vs Arthashastra.  On state power the two traditions differ in emphasis: the  Dharmashastra  (Manu) subordinates  danda to dharma  — power is exercised to uphold the moral/cosmic order, and the king is bound by Raj Dharma; the  Arthashastra  (Kautilya) makes  danda central  and dharma peripheral — material well-being (‘artha’) is ‘supreme’, for ‘on it depend dharma, kama and moksha’. Conclusion.  Kautilya is a realist like Machiavelli but a  dharma-bounded  one — which is why the Arthashastra represents a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics, where power is real and ruthless yet ultimately answerable to a higher moral order. Q — Examine the salient features of Buddhist political thought, assess whether it gave a greater ethical foundation to ancient Indian thought, and compare it with the Hindu tradition. (UPSC 2021) Gist — the spine to recall Buddhism is called the ‘rebel child of Hinduism’ — egalitarian, rational and republican. Its state arises from human corruption, and its king is ELECTED (MahaSammat) — an early social contract and ‘primus inter pares’. It rules by Dhamma (ethical persuasion), not force; the Chakravartin ‘wins hearts’ rather than land. So it gives a stronger ETHICAL, deliberative and anti-caste foundation than the hierarchical Hindu tradition. Model Answer Bhikhu Parekh calls Buddhism ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’ — an  egalitarian, rationalist and republican  tradition, the ‘Protestantism of the East’ that challenged caste. Scholars like Gail Omvedt treat the Buddha as a genuine political philosopher. Origin of state and king.  Unlike the Hindu ‘arajakta’, the Buddhist state arises from the  moral fall/corruption  of men; and the king is  elected  by consensus in the  MahaSammat  — ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’. This gives Buddhism early ideas of  decentralised democracy, equality and the social contract . Rule by Dhamma.  Government is by  Dhamma  — ethical persuasion — not by danda; the ideal  Chakravartin  ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’, i.e. wins hearts rather than conquering land. Ashoka’s polity embodied this, yet he ‘never made Buddhism a state religion’ — an implicit secularism.  Amartya Sen  praises its ‘foundational commitment to public communication and discussion’ — a deliberative ethos. Buddhist vs Hindu.  The text contrasts them: this-worldly vs other-worldly;  republican vs monarchical ; king elected by MahaSammat vs king of divine personality; winning hearts (Chakravartin) vs acquiring land; Dhamma/Panchsheel vs Danda/Mandala; and, crucially,  rejection of caste (equality)  vs Brahmanical hierarchy. Conclusion.  Buddhist thought did lend a greater  ethical and deliberative  foundation to ancient Indian political thought — egalitarian, rational and consent-based — anticipating ideas that the West reached only much later, which is precisely why  Ambedkar  chose it as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism. Q — Assess Sir Syed Ahmed Khan as a social reformer and modernizer, tracing his transition from champion of Hindu-Muslim unity to originator of the two-nation theory. (UPSC 2021/2013) Gist — the spine to recall Sir Syed believed Muslims could rise only by modernizing — embracing science and English education. As a reformer he founded MAO College (later Aligarh Muslim University) and opposed purdah, polygamy and irrationalism. Phase 1: he preached Hindu-Muslim unity — the ‘two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’. Phase 2: fearing Hindu-majority domination in elections, he opposed representative government and became the originator of the two-nation theory. Model Answer Sir Syed Ahmed Khan held that Muslim upliftment was ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, which he saw as ‘most compatible with science and rationality’ — ‘the Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’. As reformer and modernizer.  He launched the journal  Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq , a scientific society, and the  MAO College  (which became Aligarh Muslim University). A ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’, he attacked religious intolerance and denounced ‘purdah, polygamy and easy divorce’. His status among Muslims is compared to Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s among Hindus. Phase 1 — Hindu-Muslim unity.  Initially he stressed a common Indian nationhood: Hindus and Muslims are ‘the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’, sharing ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’. By ‘qaum’ he meant ‘both Hindus and Muslims’, and he worked with Hindu leaders. Phase 2 — the two-nation theory.  Fearing that in a  representative/electoral  system the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, he turned against parliamentary self-government, opposed the Congress, and sought an ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’ — becoming the originator of the  two-nation theory . The transition was driven by the Urdu-Hindi controversy, the need for government funding for his college, and rising Hindu revivalism. Conclusion.  Sir Syed was a genuine modernizer who dragged a conservative community toward science and education, but his later communal politics laid the ideological seed of Partition — a reformer whose educational legacy and political legacy pull in opposite directions. Q — Analyse Sri Aurobindo’s theory of cultural/spiritual nationalism, his conception of Swaraj and his idea of freedom. (UPSC 2017/2016/2014/2013) Gist — the spine to recall Aurobindo fused nationalism with spirituality — India is not just a land but a living Mother with a divine mission. ‘Nationalism is not a mere political programme but a way of life like religion.’ He was the first to define Swaraj as complete independence (Purna Swaraj), a precondition for India’s spiritual destiny. Real freedom for him is ‘inner freedom’ — not just political liberty but self-realisation. Model Answer Sri Aurobindo ‘connected nationalism with spirituality’; Romain Rolland saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’. In his extremist phase he rejected the Moderates’ constitutionalism and pioneered a theory of  passive resistance  that prepared the ground for Gandhi. Cultural / spiritual nationalism.  Applying the German (Herder) idea that ‘the nation is natural and has a spirit’, and inspired by Bankim’s vision of  Mother India as Goddess  and Vivekananda’s Neo-Vedanta, Aurobindo held: ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the  nation is a faith, the nation is a religion, the nation has a spirit ’. India has a ‘divine mission’ to give spirituality to the world. Swaraj.  He was the first to interpret Swaraj as  Purna Swaraj  — complete independence — pursued through swadeshi, boycott and national education. ‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’; to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’ — Swaraj is the ‘necessary condition for India to accomplish its destined goal’. Idea of freedom.  He found the liberal (anarchic) view ‘mechanical’ and the socialist view neglectful of the individual; real freedom is  inner freedom  — ‘obeying the law of our own existence’ (swadharma). His later thought turned to  Sacchidananda, the Supermind and Integral Yoga , making national self-realisation a stage toward humanity’s spiritual evolution. Conclusion.  Aurobindo raised nationalism from a political programme to a spiritual vocation. Critics call his spiritual nationalism reactionary and idealistic, yet by rooting freedom in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma and insisting on Purna Swaraj, he decisively radicalised the Indian freedom movement. Q — Evaluate Ambedkar’s idea of social justice — annihilation of caste, critique of Hinduism and of Marxism, and his conception of social/economic/political democracy — comparing his egalitarian justice with Rawls. (UPSC 2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) Gist — the spine to recall Ambedkar’s central mission was the ‘annihilation of caste’ — caste is not division of labour but ‘division of labourers’. He held Hinduism = Brahmanism, sanctified by texts like Manusmriti, so he finally converted to Buddhism. He demanded social + economic democracy, not just political — ‘political democracy cannot last without social democracy’. His justice is egalitarian/outcome-focused (uplift the depressed), going beyond Rawls’ procedural ‘justice as fairness’. Model Answer Ambedkar, ‘chief architect of the Constitution’ and himself born a Mahar, made the  annihilation of caste  his central concern. Caste, he argued in  Annihilation of Caste , is ‘not the division of labour but the division of labourers’, held together by  endogamy . Critique of Hinduism.  ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, sanctified by the Vedas and Manusmriti (on which he would ‘put dynamite’); finding no reform possible from within, he  converted to Buddhism  (1956) — ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’. Democracy.  For Ambedkar democracy is ‘a way of life’ resting on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’. He insisted on completing  political democracy with social and economic democracy : ‘we must make our political democracy a social democracy as well; political democracy cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy’ — secured through  constitutional morality  and ‘state socialism’. Critique of Marxism.  He rejected two Marxist claims: that religion is mere ‘opium’ (Buddhism, based on karuna, samata and prajna, is not), and that the state is the chief oppressor — for Ambedkar ‘society is more exploitative than the state’, so the state must be an instrument of emancipation. Ambedkar vs Rawls.  Ambedkar’s social justice is  egalitarian and outcome-oriented  — actively uplifting the depressed classes through state action — whereas Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ is  procedural , built on a hypothetical original position. Ambedkar starts from real historical injustice, not an abstract veil of ignorance. Conclusion.  Ambedkar transformed the idea of justice in India from a matter of procedure into one of  substantive social emancipation , making the annihilation of caste and the completion of democracy through social and economic equality his enduring legacy. Q — Trace M.N. Roy’s ideational journey from Marxism to Radical Humanism, and identify the major components of Modern Indian Political Thought with reference to Gandhi and Roy. Gist — the spine to recall Roy moved from nationalism → communism → finally ‘radical humanism’. He broke with Lenin (the colonies’ revolution debate) and then with Marxism itself for subduing the individual. Radical Humanism = reason + morality + freedom, centred on the individual, not the class or party. He rejected the party system for ‘party-less’ radical democracy — small self-governing ‘people’s committees’. Model Answer M.N. Roy’s intellectual life moved through three phases —  nationalism → communism → radical humanism . A founder of the CPI, he clashed with  Lenin  at the Comintern (1920): against Lenin’s two-stage strategy of allying with bourgeois-nationalist parties, Roy’s  Supplementary Theses  argued that communists must lead the colonial proletariat directly — ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’. Break with Marxism.  Disillusioned, Roy came to see ‘Marxism as more method than dogma’ and criticised it on several counts: it  subdues individualism  (‘the collective ego of the proletariat’); historical materialism is mere ‘economic determinism’; and the sanction for ending exploitation is ‘not economic but  moral ’. Radical Humanism.  His  New Humanism: A Manifesto  rests on three elements —  Reason  (rejecting blind faith),  Morality  (secular, rational) and  Freedom  (‘the progressive removal of all restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’). He envisioned a cosmopolitan ‘commonwealth of spiritually free men’. Party-less radical democracy.  Holding that the party system ‘bred social and political immorality’ and reduced sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’, Roy dissolved his own party (1948) for ‘organized democracy’ — decentralised ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’, with primacy to the individual. Modern Indian Political Thought — Gandhi and Roy.  Its major components are visible in the contrast between  Gandhi  (spiritual, religion as a moralising force, decentralised Ram Rajya, non-violence) and  Roy  (rationalist-humanist, secular, individual-centred, party-less democracy) — both, however, converge on  decentralisation, the primacy of the individual/community, and morality in politics . Conclusion.  Though Bidyut Chakraborty judged Roy ‘unable to free himself entirely from Marxism’, Roy’s radical humanism brought a genuinely fresh, individual-centred and cosmopolitan voice to modern Indian political thought.
